question: What proportion of children and young people assessed by CAMHS or crisis services after self-harm are referred to an age-appropriate crisis response service (or equivalent specialist mental health professional) for a psychosocial assessment as soon as possible after arrival?
why: No closed-loop audit of psychosocial assessment referral for self-harm restricted to under-18s in a crisis or CAMHS pathway has been published in the library; existing self-harm audits in children and young people measure assessment content and timing at a single site rather than whether the crisis pathway referral itself happens.

standard.source: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, rec 1.7.13 (September 2022)
standard.wording: When a person attends the emergency department or minor injury unit following an episode of self-harm, offer referral to age-appropriate liaison psychiatry services, or for children and young people, crisis response service (or an equivalent specialist mental health service or a suitably skilled mental health professional) as soon as possible after arrival, for a psychosocial assessment ... and support and assistance alongside physical healthcare.

population: Inclusion: patients aged under 18 attending the emergency department or minor injuries unit after an episode of self-harm. Exclusion: attendances for accidental injury only, or where the person left before triage.
sample: 30 consecutive under-18 self-harm attendances to the emergency department over the last 3 months, identified from the ED self-harm coding list
data_source: ED electronic record (triage note, referral log) cross-checked against the CAMHS/crisis team referral log

template.note: Study ID, not the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'crisis response/CAMHS referral made: time' field to the ED self-harm triage template, which cannot be closed without either a referral time or a documented reason none was needed
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size, from the ED self-harm coding list
close_loop: Present at the paediatric emergency department and CAMHS joint governance meeting; if the change works, embed the mandatory field as a permanent build in the ED electronic record and add it to ED junior doctor induction
evidence: [3174] Paediatric psychosocial emergencies audit against NICE self-harm quality standards: 93% seen within 24 hours of referral, 97% had a documented risk assessment, showing referral pathways can be measured and improved with a dedicated crisis liaison nurse

[3392] National student-led SPARC audit of ED management of self-harm in under-18s: a quarter of records were excluded for data quality issues, showing referral documentation is often incomplete and worth auditing directly
pitfalls: Referral may happen by phone/bleep with no written record: agree with the crisis team in advance that every referral is also logged electronically
Patients who abscond before triage or assessment are not comparable: exclude them explicitly and report the number excluded
Staff may push back that 'we always refer everyone': collect a baseline before assuming this, since local card CR-3174/3392 show gaps even where staff believe compliance is high
A single term for the crisis service may not match every trust's naming: agree the exact service name with the ED and CAMHS leads before data collection starts
Out-of-hours attendances may use a different on-call pathway: capture time of day so out-of-hours performance can be reported separately
pearls: Recruit an ED consultant and a CAMHS/crisis team consultant as joint audit leads so the fix can be built into both systems
Agree before cycle 1 exactly what counts as 'referral made' (a bleep call, an electronic referral, or both)
Use the ED's existing self-harm coding list to identify the sample quickly rather than manually screening all attendances
Present the baseline to both teams together so the fix is owned jointly, not seen as an ED-only or CAMHS-only problem
Hand the audit and the mandatory-field build to the incoming CAMHS liaison trainee at rotation, with the re-audit date fixed in the departmental audit calendar
effort: ~25 min per 10 attendances from the ED record and referral log
pass: Referral to the crisis response service (or equivalent) is documented as made, with the time of referral recorded, for every under-18 self-harm attendance

question: What proportion of children and young people are seen and spoken to by an age-appropriate liaison psychiatry professional or a suitably skilled mental health professional at every attendance to the emergency department following an episode of self-harm?
why: Existing self-harm audits in the library report overall assessment rates at a single attendance; none in the library measure whether this happens at every attendance for young people who self-harm repeatedly, which NICE specifically requires.

standard.source: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, rec 1.7.14 (September 2022)
standard.wording: An age-appropriate liaison psychiatry professional or a suitably skilled mental health professional should see and speak to the person at every attendance after an episode of self-harm.

population: Inclusion: patients aged under 18 with two or more ED attendances for self-harm in the audit period. Exclusion: patients with a single attendance only (nothing to compare).
sample: All under-18 patients with 2 or more self-harm attendances in the last 6 months (typically 30-40 attendances across a district general hospital), identified from the ED self-harm coding list
data_source: ED electronic record and mental health liaison team notes for each attendance
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic flag on the ED tracking board for any patient with a previous self-harm attendance in the last 6 months, prompting mandatory liaison review even if the presentation looks minor
reaudit: At 4 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the CAMHS/liaison psychiatry governance meeting; if effective, build the repeat-attendance flag permanently into the ED electronic patient record
evidence: [3403] Multicentre UK audit of clinical management of self-harming children and adolescents against the NICE self-harm guideline for young people aged 8 and over, showing management of repeat presentations is an established audit focus but not yet closed-loop in the library
pitfalls: Repeat attenders may be seen by different professionals each time, fragmenting the record: search by patient identifier across all attendances, not by single episode
'Suitably skilled mental health professional' is not defined locally: agree a short list of qualifying roles with CAMHS before data collection
Attendances that end in the young person leaving before assessment will look like a 'fail' for reasons outside the team's control: record and report separately
Staff may see repeat self-harm as 'attention seeking' and be less thorough: present the data without individual blame and focus on the system flag
Six months may be too short to find repeat attenders in a small unit: extend the window rather than lowering the sample size
pearls: Ask the ED data team to run the repeat-attendance search electronically rather than manually cross-referencing notes
Recruit the CAMHS lead nurse to help define 'suitably skilled' before cycle 1 so there is no dispute at analysis
Share the individual (anonymised) attendance timelines with the team, not just the percentage, as this is the most persuasive way to show gaps
Agree with IT in advance whether the repeat-attendance flag can be built as an automatic alert, since this is what worked in comparable services
Keep the audit with the liaison team rather than a rotating CAMHS trainee, since continuity of care is the point being measured
effort: ~30 min per 10 attendances, more if cross-referencing across services
pass: A note from an age-appropriate liaison psychiatry professional or suitably skilled mental health professional is present for that specific attendance

question: What proportion of children and young people assessed by mental health services after self-harm have a written safety plan for future episodes, developed and agreed with them, documented before they leave the assessment?
why: No audit in the library measures whether a collaborative written safety plan (as opposed to a generic risk score or care plan) is produced for children and young people who self-harm.

standard.source: NICE NG225 Self-harm: assessment, management and preventing recurrence, rec 1.5.14 (September 2022)
standard.wording: developing a safety plan for future episodes of self-harm, which should be written with and agreed by the person who self-harms.

population: Inclusion: patients aged under 18 assessed by CAMHS, crisis or liaison services after an episode of self-harm. Exclusion: assessments that were not completed (patient left, or admitted for medical reasons before assessment could finish).
sample: 30 consecutive completed self-harm psychosocial assessments in under-18s over the last 3 months
data_source: CAMHS/crisis team electronic assessment record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Replace the free-text 'plan' box in the self-harm assessment template with a structured safety plan template (warning signs, coping strategies, contacts, means restriction) that must be completed and printed or shared with the young person before the assessment can be closed
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample size
close_loop: Present at the CAMHS clinical governance meeting; if the template raises completion, make it the mandatory default in the electronic record
evidence: [3174] Paediatric psychosocial emergencies audit against NICE self-harm quality standards found 92% had a 7-day follow-up review after a dedicated crisis liaison model was introduced, showing structured follow-up processes are achievable but a dedicated safety-plan-specific audit has not been published
pitfalls: A generic 'risk management plan' may be wrongly counted as a safety plan: define the required elements (triggers, coping strategies, contacts) in the data collection tool
Assessments completed out of hours by a duty worker may use a paper safety plan that is not scanned into the electronic record: check both paper and electronic sources
Families may decline to be involved: record this as a valid reason rather than a failure of the young person's own agreement
Clinicians may feel a template is too rigid for individual presentations: pilot the template with two or three clinicians and gather feedback before full rollout
Improvement may fade once the pilot team's enthusiasm wears off: build the template into the mandatory record rather than relying on a reminder poster
pearls: Base the template on an existing published safety-planning tool (e.g. a suicide safety plan format) rather than designing one from scratch
Involve a young person or family representative in reviewing the template wording before rollout
Agree with reception/admin that the safety plan can be printed on the spot so families leave with a physical copy
Present both the completion rate and a couple of anonymised examples of good versus poor plans to help clinicians see what 'good' looks like
Hand ownership of the re-audit to the CAMHS or crisis team's own quality improvement lead rather than a single trainee, since teams rotate
effort: ~15 min per 10 assessments from the CAMHS record
pass: A safety plan document exists in the record for that assessment, is dated, and states it was agreed with the young person

question: What proportion of children and young people on ADHD medication have their height and weight measured at the intervals specified by NICE (height every 6 months; weight every 3 months if aged 10 or under, or at 3 and 6 months then every 6 months if older)?
why: No closed-loop audit in the library measures compliance with the exact NICE NG87 growth-monitoring schedule for children and young people on ADHD medication; existing CAMHS prescribing audits in the corpus measure prescribing quality generally, not this specific monitoring interval.

standard.source: NICE NG87 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management, rec 1.8.5 (2018)
standard.wording: For people taking medication for ADHD: measure height every 6 months in children and young people measure weight every 3 months in children 10 years and under measure weight at 3 and 6 months after starting treatment in children over 10 years and young people, and every 6 months thereafter, or more often if concerns arise ... plot height and weight of children and young people on a growth chart and ensure review by the healthcare professional responsible for treatment.

population: Inclusion: patients aged under 18 currently prescribed a stimulant or non-stimulant ADHD medication for at least 6 months. Exclusion: patients started on medication in the last 3 months (too early to judge the schedule).
sample: 40 consecutive children and young people on ADHD medication for at least 6 months, from the CAMHS/paediatric ADHD clinic caseload
data_source: CAMHS or paediatric ADHD clinic electronic record and growth chart
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build an automatic reminder into the ADHD clinic appointment system that flags when height or weight is due, and require the growth chart to auto-populate from the recorded measurements
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the CAMHS or community paediatrics governance meeting; if effective, embed the automatic reminder as a permanent build
evidence: Topic card 'ADHD medication monitoring' (11 audits in the library): six-monthly weight, pulse and blood pressure are the weak point, with recording as low as 8-19% [3198] and only 30.9% monitored within NICE intervals [3622]; a dedicated ADHD clinic and shared-care process raised annual BP monitoring from 62.0% to 90.4% and weight from 56.7% to 80.3% [3527]
pitfalls: Height and weight recorded at a GP or school nurse visit outside the ADHD clinic may be missed: agree a single source of truth for measurements before starting
A telephone or video review cannot include physical measurements: record whether the appointment was face-to-face and exclude remote reviews from the numerator
The interval differs by age band (under 10 vs over 10): pre-sort the sample by age so the correct schedule is applied to each patient
Teaching alone rarely moves this measure, as the library shows an electronic record change is needed to convert centiles automatically
Non-attendance at review appointments will look like a monitoring gap: record DNAs separately from measurements not taken at an attended appointment
pearls: Recruit the ADHD clinic administrator to help build the automatic reminder, since they control the appointment system
Agree the exact NICE interval definitions with the clinic team before data collection to avoid disputes at analysis
Use the growth chart itself (not just a text entry) as the source of truth, since a plotted point is easy to verify
Share the topic card's finding that a dedicated clinic model (not teaching) achieved the biggest gains, to set expectations for the fix
Timetable the re-audit for after the reminder system has been running for a full monitoring cycle (6 months), not sooner
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the ADHD clinic record
pass: Height and weight are both recorded at the NICE-specified interval for the child's age and plotted on a growth chart

question: What proportion of children, young people and adults on ADHD medication have their heart rate and blood pressure measured and compared with the normal range for age before and after each dose change, and at least every 6 months?
why: No closed-loop audit in the library isolates cardiovascular monitoring at dose change specifically (as opposed to routine periodic monitoring); the topic card for ADHD medication monitoring shows this remains the weakest single measure in the corpus.

standard.source: NICE NG87 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management, rec 1.8.9 (2018)
standard.wording: Monitor heart rate and blood pressure and compare with the normal range for age before and after each dose change and every 6 months.

population: Inclusion: patients of any age on ADHD medication with at least one dose change in the last 12 months. Exclusion: patients with no dose change in that period, audited under the routine 6-monthly measure only.
sample: 40 consecutive patients on ADHD medication with a dose change in the last 12 months, from the ADHD clinic caseload (CAMHS, adult ADHD service or shared care)
data_source: ADHD clinic electronic record, dose change log and observation chart
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Link the ADHD e-prescribing dose-change order to a mandatory observation set, so the prescription cannot be finalised without a recorded heart rate and blood pressure compared against the age-normal range
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the ADHD service governance meeting; if the mandatory link works, extend it to all ADHD prescribers including shared-care GPs
evidence: Topic card 'ADHD medication monitoring': centiles are rarely used (BP 10%, HR 0% in one sample [3525]); presenting results alone raised weight monitoring from 15% to 45% and HR from 8% to 40% [3198], but teaching and posters did not move BP or HR centiles because the record could not convert them automatically [3525]
pitfalls: Recording a raw heart rate/BP without comparing to the age-normal range should not count as a pass: define 'compared' as an explicit centile or normal/abnormal statement in the data tool
Dose changes made by a shared-care GP may not be visible to the specialist service: include a data-sharing check with primary care before starting
The library shows posters and teaching failed here because the electronic system could not calculate centiles: budget for an IT change, not just an education session
Patients who decline monitoring should be recorded as a specific category, not counted as a system failure
Multiple small dose titrations in a short period could be double-counted: use the most recent dose change in the audit period as the index event
pearls: Involve the electronic prescribing/IT team from the outset, since the library shows a system fix (not teaching) is what worked elsewhere
Use an age-appropriate blood pressure centile calculator built into or linked from the record, rather than a paper chart
Present the topic card evidence (teaching failed, system change worked) to secure sign-off for an IT change request
Pilot the mandatory link with one prescriber before rolling out trust-wide, to catch workflow problems early
Fix the re-audit date at 6 months so at least one full monitoring cycle has passed since the change
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the ADHD clinic record and dose change log
pass: Heart rate and blood pressure are recorded and compared with the normal range for age, both at the most recent dose change and at the most recent 6-monthly review

question: What proportion of children and young people on ADHD medication whose blood pressure is consistently above the 95th centile for age and height are referred to a paediatric hypertension specialist before medication is continued?
why: No audit in the library links an abnormal blood pressure finding on ADHD medication to the specific referral action NICE requires; the ADHD monitoring topic card shows measurement is already poor, and no audit in the corpus checks what happens once a high reading is found.

standard.source: NICE NG87 Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management, rec 1.7.6 (2018)
standard.wording: Refer to a paediatric hypertension specialist before starting medication for ADHD if blood pressure is consistently above the 95th centile for age and height for children and young people.

population: Inclusion: patients aged under 18 on ADHD medication with at least one blood pressure reading above the 95th centile for age/height in the last 12 months, confirmed on a repeat reading. Exclusion: an isolated single high reading not repeated.
sample: All identified cases in the last 12 months from the ADHD clinic caseload (expect approximately 15-25 cases in a typical CAMHS/paediatric ADHD service, given the low rate of BP centile use found elsewhere in the corpus)
data_source: ADHD clinic electronic record and hypertension/cardiology referral log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic alert in the electronic record that fires when a blood pressure centile is entered above the 95th centile for an ADHD patient, prompting an immediate referral order
reaudit: At 12 months, same template, widened sample if fewer than 15 cases found
close_loop: Present at the ADHD/paediatric cardiology joint meeting; if the alert works, keep it as a permanent build
evidence: Topic card 'ADHD medication monitoring': centiles are rarely used at all (BP 10%, HR 0% in one sample [3525]), so an audit specifically of the referral pathway once a high reading is found has not been done in the library
pitfalls: If BP centiles are rarely calculated in the first place (as the library shows), the true denominator of 'confirmed high BP' may be undercounted: report the number of patients with any BP centile recorded alongside the audit result
A single high reading without repeat measurement should not count towards the denominator: require a second confirmatory reading before counting a case
Referral pathways to paediatric hypertension services vary between trusts: confirm the correct local referral route before data collection
Cases may be too few for a stable percentage: report as a proportion with the raw numerator and denominator, not just a percentage
Prescribers may continue medication while awaiting referral without recording a reason: capture this explicitly rather than assuming an oversight
pearls: Work with the ADHD clinic's admin team to search the record for any BP centile entries above the 95th centile, since these cases are rare and easy to miss manually
Agree the referral pathway and target response time with paediatric cardiology/hypertension before cycle 1
Because numbers will be small, present individual case summaries (anonymised) alongside the percentage to make the point clearly
Build the alert as a hard stop or strong prompt in the electronic record, since a soft reminder is unlikely to succeed given how rarely centiles are used
Keep this audit running continuously (rather than a single cycle) since new high-BP cases will appear slowly over time
effort: ~15 min per identified case from the clinic record and referral log
pass: A referral to a paediatric hypertension specialist is documented within 4 weeks of the blood pressure being confirmed as consistently above the 95th centile

question: What proportion of adults with a learning disability newly started on a psychotropic medication for behaviour that challenges have a documented plan for reducing or stopping the medication, with a target timescale?
why: The STOMP topic card (13 audits in the library) shows a reduce/stop plan is recorded in only 10-17% of cases [3685] and a stopping timescale in 29% [3445]; the consultant advice is to audit whether a reduce-or-stop plan with a timescale exists, which no library audit currently isolates as its own question.

standard.source: NICE NG11 Challenging behaviour and learning disabilities, rec 1.8.5 (2015)
standard.wording: Ensure that the following are documented: a rationale for medication (explained to the person with a learning disability and everyone involved in their care, including their family members and carers) how long the medication should be taken for a strategy for reviewing the prescription and stopping the medication.

population: Inclusion: adults with a learning disability newly started (in the last 12 months) on an antipsychotic, antidepressant, anticonvulsant used as a mood stabiliser, benzodiazepine or hypnotic for behaviour that challenges. Exclusion: medication started for a diagnosed mental illness rather than behaviour that challenges.
sample: 30 consecutive adults with a learning disability newly started on a psychotropic for behaviour that challenges in the last 12 months, from the community learning disability team or STOMP register
data_source: Community learning disability team electronic record and medication review documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'planned duration and stopping strategy' field to the STOMP medication initiation template, which must be completed before the prescription can be signed
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the community learning disability team governance meeting; if the mandatory field works, adopt it trust-wide for all STOMP-relevant prescriptions
evidence: [3685] STOMP audit found a documented reduce/stop plan in only 10-17% of cases
[3445] STOMP audit found a timescale for stopping medication documented in 29% of cases

[3268] Repeated audit cycles in one intellectual disability team raised metabolic monitoring from 0% to 95% and risk assessment from 68% to 100%, showing repeated cycles with a fixed template can close this gap
pitfalls: A generic 'review in clinic' note without a specific date or trigger should not count as a pass: define this precisely in the data tool
New starters may be prescribed by an out-of-area or private provider whose notes are not available: exclude and record these separately
Staff may see stopping plans as unrealistic for long-standing behaviour: present the audit as measuring documentation of intent, not a requirement to actually stop
The library shows side-effect discussion fell after criteria changed between cycles in one service [3416]: keep the same criteria across both cycles
Family or paid carers may not be present at review to discuss stopping: record whether they were consulted, as this affects the quality of the plan
pearls: Base the mandatory field on the exact NG11 1.8.5 wording so there is no ambiguity about what counts as a strategy
Recruit the learning disability pharmacist to help design and monitor the field, since they typically run the STOMP register
Share the topic card's consultant advice (count actual dose reductions, not just plans) directly with the team to set the improvement target
Time the re-audit to align with the annual STOMP reporting cycle already required by NHS England, so data collection is not duplicated
Keep the audit register with the learning disability team pharmacist rather than a rotating psychiatry trainee, for continuity
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the STOMP register and clinic notes
pass: The record states how long the medication should be taken for and a strategy for reviewing and stopping it, with a specific target date or trigger

question: Of adults with a learning disability prescribed an antipsychotic for behaviour that challenges with a documented review of effectiveness, what proportion with no indication of response by 6 weeks have the medication actually stopped or the decision to continue explicitly justified in writing?
why: The STOMP topic card explicitly advises counting actual dose reductions and stopping, not just whether a review plan exists; no audit in the library measures the real-world action taken once the 6-week review point is reached.

standard.source: NICE NG11 Challenging behaviour and learning disabilities, rec 1.8.4 (2015)
standard.wording: stop the medication if there is no indication of a response at 6 weeks, reassess the behaviour that challenges and consider further psychological or environmental interventions.

population: Inclusion: adults with a learning disability on an antipsychotic for behaviour that challenges, with a documented 6-week (or later) effectiveness review. Exclusion: patients on antipsychotics for a diagnosed psychotic illness.
sample: 30 consecutive adults with a learning disability on antipsychotics for behaviour that challenges who have passed their 6-week review point, from the community learning disability team caseload
data_source: Community learning disability team electronic record and medication review notes
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a hard-stop prompt in the electronic prescribing system at the 6-week point for any antipsychotic coded as 'for behaviour that challenges', requiring either a stop order or a written justification before the prescription can be continued
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the community learning disability team and pharmacy governance meeting; if effective, extend the 6-week prompt to all STOMP-relevant prescriptions
evidence: [3584] STOMP audit found no clear indication for 50.6% of antipsychotics prescribed for behaviour that challenges
[3416] Side-effect discussion at initiation fell from 73% to 38% after review criteria changed between cycles, showing the review process itself needs a fixed template to hold gains
pitfalls: 'No clear response' may be under-recorded because staff default to continuing rather than actively reassessing: define the audit to flag any review note lacking an explicit response statement as a fail
Environmental or psychological interventions may be tried without being recorded as linked to the medication review: cross-check care plans as well as prescription notes
Carers and care home staff may resist stopping medication they believe is working: record any documented carer view as part of the justification, not as an automatic pass
A change of prescriber partway through the period could mean the 6-week review was never formally handed over: check for a gap in responsibility
Numbers may be small in a single team: consider a longer collection window or pooling across neighbouring learning disability teams
pearls: Use the exact NG11 wording ('no indication of a response at 6 weeks') as the pass/fail definition to avoid subjective judgement calls
Involve a learning disability nurse or support worker who knows the person well in the review, since they can describe real behavioural change
Present the finding alongside the topic card's headline gap (50.6% with no clear indication [3584]) to show this is a known, high-harm, fixable problem
Agree the pharmacy hard-stop build with IT and pharmacy governance before cycle 1 so the change can go live immediately after presentation
Track actual dose reductions and stops at re-audit, not just documentation, as this is what the topic card identifies as missing from every existing audit
effort: ~20 min per 10 patients from the STOMP register and prescribing record
pass: The medication is stopped by 6 weeks if there is no indication of response, or, if continued, a specific written justification for continuing is present in the notes

question: What proportion of adults with a learning disability have an annual health check that includes a review of mental health problems?
why: No audit in the library measures the mental health component of the learning disability annual health check specifically, despite this being a distinct NICE quality statement; existing corpus audits on learning disability focus on medication (STOMP) and physical monitoring, not the annual check itself.

standard.source: NICE QS142 Learning disability: identifying and managing mental health problems, quality statement 1 (10 January 2017)
standard.wording: Young people and adults with a learning disability have an annual health check that includes a review of mental health problems.

population: Inclusion: adults on the GP learning disability register who had an annual health check in the last 12 months. Exclusion: people who declined the annual health check.
sample: 40 consecutive annual health checks completed in the last 12 months, from the GP learning disability register at one or two participating practices
data_source: GP electronic record (annual health check template)
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory mental health review section to the GP annual health check template (already used for the learning disability DES), which cannot be marked complete without an entry
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample, timed to the next annual health check cycle
close_loop: Present at the primary care network or practice clinical governance meeting; if effective, embed the mandatory field trust/practice-wide
evidence: No audit of the mental health component of the learning disability annual health check is recorded in the library; the closest related entries concern STOMP medication review [3685] and antipsychotic physical health monitoring, not the annual check itself
pitfalls: Annual health checks are often nurse-led using a template that may not prompt for mental health explicitly: check the template itself as well as individual entries
A tick-box 'mental health: normal' with no detail may be too weak to count as a real review: agree with the primary care team what counts as adequate detail before data collection
People who decline or do not attend are excluded from this audit but should be tracked separately, since non-attendance is itself a known access problem
GP data systems vary (EMIS, SystmOne): the exact template location for annual health checks will differ between practices
A learning disability nurse or GP may feel this adds to an already long consultation: build the change into the existing template rather than adding a separate step
pearls: Work with the practice's learning disability register lead, who already runs the annual health check DES, to make this change with minimal extra burden
Use a short, validated question (for example, a simple mood and behaviour change screen) rather than a lengthy new tool
Present the audit to the primary care network learning disability lead, since a template change there can spread across several practices at once
Agree in advance how referral for a mental health concern found at the check will be actioned (to the community learning disability team), so the change closes a real loop
Fix the re-audit to the next annual health check cycle so the same patients can be tracked over time
effort: ~15 min per 10 records from the GP annual health check template
pass: The annual health check record includes an explicit mental health review (a question, screening tool result, or narrative comment on mental state), not just physical health items

question: What proportion of adults with a learning disability referred for a mental health assessment are seen by a professional with specific expertise in mental health problems in people with a learning disability?
why: No audit in the library measures whether learning disability mental health referrals reach an appropriately expert assessor, as opposed to generic community mental health team triage.

standard.source: NICE QS142 Learning disability: identifying and managing mental health problems, quality statement 2 (10 January 2017)
standard.wording: People with a learning disability who need a mental health assessment are referred to a professional with expertise in mental health problems in people with learning disabilities.

population: Inclusion: adults with a learning disability referred for a mental health assessment in the last 12 months. Exclusion: referrals for a physical health problem only.
sample: 30 consecutive learning disability mental health referrals in the last 12 months, from the community learning disability team or generic community mental health team referral log
data_source: Community mental health/learning disability team referral and assessment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic flag on the community mental health team referral system that redirects any referral coded 'learning disability' to the specialist learning disability team, or requires documented learning disability liaison input if seen elsewhere
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the joint community learning disability/mental health team governance meeting; if effective, keep the automatic redirect as a permanent build
evidence: Related entries concern STOMP medication review [3685] and metabolic monitoring in one intellectual disability team [3268], but no library audit yet measures the referral-to-specialist-assessor pathway itself
pitfalls: A generic community mental health team may see the person without recognising the learning disability, especially if mild: check the referral coding as well as the outcome
Rural or smaller services may have no dedicated learning disability specialist and rely on liaison input: define what counts as adequate liaison before data collection
Referral letters may not state the person has a learning disability if it is not the presenting reason: cross-check against the GP learning disability register
Waiting times to a specialist team may be longer than to a generic team, creating pressure to bypass the specialist route: record time to assessment for both
Historic referrals may predate a service reorganisation: use only referrals from the last 12 months to reflect current pathways
pearls: Cross-reference the referral list against the GP learning disability register to make sure no relevant referral is missed
Agree a single definition of 'learning disability expertise' with both teams before starting, to avoid disputes over borderline cases
Recruit a joint audit lead from both the learning disability and generic mental health teams so the fix is owned by both
Use the audit findings to support a business case for a formal liaison arrangement if none currently exists
Keep the referral log query script so the re-audit can be run quickly by whoever holds the audit next
effort: ~15 min per 10 referrals from the referral and assessment record
pass: The assessing clinician is a psychiatrist, nurse or psychologist with a learning disability specialism (community learning disability team, or a generic mental health service with documented learning disability liaison input)

question: What proportion of adults with a learning disability and a serious mental illness have a named key worker recorded in their care plan to coordinate their care?
why: No audit in the library measures whether people with a learning disability and serious mental illness have a single named key worker, despite this being a specific NICE quality statement distinct from general care planning audits already in the corpus.

standard.source: NICE QS142 Learning disability: identifying and managing mental health problems, quality statement 3 (10 January 2017)
standard.wording: People with a learning disability and a serious mental illness have a key worker to coordinate their care.

population: Inclusion: adults with a learning disability and a diagnosed serious mental illness (psychosis, bipolar disorder or severe depression) open to community learning disability or mental health services. Exclusion: people not currently open to a community team.
sample: 30 consecutive adults with a learning disability and serious mental illness on the current community learning disability/mental health caseload
data_source: Community learning disability/mental health team electronic care plan
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'named key worker' field to the community learning disability team's care plan template, which must be completed and updated at every care plan review
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the community learning disability team governance meeting; if effective, embed as a mandatory field trust-wide
evidence: Related entries in the corpus concern general care plan documentation in mental health (topic: Care plan documentation in mental health), but no audit specifically checks the learning disability key worker requirement in QS142
pitfalls: A team may be named as 'key worker' rather than an individual, which does not meet the intent of the standard: define 'named' as a specific person in the data tool
Key workers may change with staff turnover without the care plan being updated: check the last care plan review date alongside the named worker
People open to both a community learning disability team and a separate community mental health team may have two different named workers, causing confusion: record and flag this as a fail
Caseload lists may be out of date: verify the current caseload with the team manager before sampling
Care plans stored only on paper in some services will need manual review alongside the electronic record
pearls: Agree the definition of 'serious mental illness' (psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe depression) with the team before sampling to keep the population consistent
Ask the team manager for an up-to-date caseload list rather than relying on a historic report
Present the audit alongside the QS142 statement wording so the standard is unambiguous to the team
Build the key worker field into whatever care planning software is already in use, rather than a separate document
Repeat the audit after the next round of staff changes, since key worker continuity is most at risk during turnover
effort: ~15 min per 10 records from the care plan
pass: A single named key worker is documented in the current care plan, with their role and contact details

question: What proportion of adults with a learning disability who remain on an antipsychotic medication that has not been reduced or stopped have the reasons for continuing it documented at least once in the last 12 months?
why: The antipsychotic physical health monitoring topic card in the library (39 audits) focuses on physical monitoring; no audit isolates this specific NICE requirement to justify ongoing antipsychotic use annually in learning disability, which is the STOMP overmedication review question at its core.

standard.source: NICE QS142 Learning disability: identifying and managing mental health problems, quality statement 5 (10 January 2017)
standard.wording: People with a learning disability who are taking antipsychotic drugs that are not reduced or stopped have annual documentation on reasons for continuing this prescription.

population: Inclusion: adults with a learning disability on a continuous antipsychotic prescription for more than 12 months, with no dose reduction in that period. Exclusion: patients whose dose has been reduced or who have been switched or stopped in the period.
sample: 30 consecutive adults with a learning disability on an unchanged antipsychotic dose for more than 12 months, from the community learning disability team or STOMP register
data_source: Community learning disability team electronic record and STOMP register
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an annual STOMP review reminder to the electronic record for every patient on an unchanged antipsychotic dose, which must be completed with an explicit reason for continuing before it can be dismissed
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the STOMP steering group or community learning disability team governance meeting; if effective, embed the reminder trust-wide
evidence: Topic card 'Psychotropic prescribing in learning disability (STOMP)': timescale for stopping documented in 29% of cases [3445] and a reduce/stop plan in 10-17% [3685]; consultant advice highlights that documenting a rationale at initiation is common but ongoing justification for continuing is not routinely checked
pitfalls: A brief 'continue as before' note should not count as a pass: define the required content (specific clinical reason) in the data tool
Patients seen only by a GP on a shared-care basis may not have specialist review documented at all: check both specialist and GP records
Long-stay patients with decades of unchanged prescribing may have no recent documented rationale anywhere: report this finding directly rather than assuming it exists
Staff may resist a formal reminder as bureaucratic if they know the patient well: frame the change as a safeguard against unexamined long-term prescribing, per LeDeR-type learning
A dose reduction attempted and reversed due to relapse should still count as active review, not treated the same as no review at all
pearls: Use the STOMP register (already required by NHS England) as the sampling frame so the audit does not duplicate existing data collection
Recruit the learning disability pharmacist to lead the annual reminder build and review the findings
Present the QS142 statement 5 wording directly to prescribers so the annual documentation requirement is unambiguous
Track whether annual review leads to any actual dose changes over time, not just documentation, to show real impact
Align the re-audit date with the trust's existing annual STOMP reporting deadline to avoid duplicate data pulls
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the STOMP register and clinic notes
pass: A dated entry in the last 12 months explicitly states the reason for continuing the antipsychotic

question: What proportion of women of childbearing potential newly assessed by adult or perinatal mental health services while already prescribed valproate for a mental health condition have a documented discussion of switching to an alternative medication?
why: The valproate pregnancy prevention topic card in the library (6 audits) shows documentation of the pregnancy prevention programme is poor, but the consultant advice notes that whether patients were switched to an alternative treatment is not yet audited; NICE specifically restricts valproate use in this group unless alternatives are ineffective.

standard.source: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health, rec 1.2.3 (2014, amended 2020)
standard.wording: Do not offer valproate for acute or long-term treatment of a mental health problem in women or girls of childbearing potential (including young girls who are likely to need treatment into their childbearing years), unless other options are ineffective or not tolerated and the pregnancy prevention programme is in place.

population: Inclusion: women aged 12-55 of childbearing potential newly assessed by adult or perinatal mental health services who are already prescribed valproate for a mental health condition. Exclusion: valproate prescribed solely for epilepsy under neurology.
sample: All identified cases in the last 12 months from the mental health service valproate register (typically 15-25 women in a district general hospital catchment)
data_source: Mental health service electronic record and valproate/pregnancy prevention programme register
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'alternative treatment considered' field to the mental health service's valproate register review template, which must be completed at every review of a woman of childbearing potential
reaudit: At 12 months, same template, using the updated valproate register
close_loop: Present at the trust medicines safety or perinatal mental health governance meeting; if effective, embed the mandatory field in the valproate register template trust-wide
evidence: Topic card 'Valproate pregnancy prevention programme': Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form completed in only 3% [3196] and 0% dual-signed [3656] of cases, with contraception advice as low as 0-15% [3418][3656]; consultant advice notes the gap in auditing whether patients were switched to alternatives has not yet been closed
pitfalls: Women may already be stable on valproate after multiple failed alternatives, making a switch clinically inappropriate: record this as a documented, reasoned decision rather than a fail
Perinatal and adult mental health teams may hold separate valproate registers: reconcile both before sampling to avoid double counting or missed cases
Small numbers are likely given how few women of childbearing potential remain on valproate once the pregnancy prevention programme is enforced: report raw numbers alongside any percentage
A woman may not disclose she is sexually active or planning pregnancy, affecting the urgency of the discussion: record what was asked, not assumed
Switching medication carries its own relapse risk: frame the change as ensuring the discussion happens, not mandating a switch
pearls: Use the mental health pharmacist-held valproate register as the single source of truth for the sampling frame
Involve both perinatal and adult mental health pharmacy leads, since patients often move between these services
Present the topic card's consultant advice directly to the team to justify why this specific angle (switching, not just ARAF completion) is the audit focus
Agree with the team in advance what counts as an acceptable 'alternatives ineffective or not tolerated' justification
Keep the valproate register under pharmacy ownership so the re-audit can be run without waiting for a trainee rotation
effort: ~20 min per identified case from the valproate register and clinical record
pass: The record shows either that valproate was not used, or, if it was continued, a documented trial or consideration of at least one alternative and that the pregnancy prevention programme is in place

question: What proportion of women with a current or past severe mental health problem who are planning a pregnancy are referred to a secondary mental health service, preferably a specialist perinatal mental health service, for preconception counselling?
why: No audit in the library measures preconception counselling referral for women with severe mental illness planning pregnancy; existing perinatal audits in the corpus concern administrative recording and GP referral processes, not this specific preconception pathway.

standard.source: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health, rec 1.4.2 (2014)
standard.wording: Consider referring a woman to a secondary mental health service (preferably a specialist perinatal mental health service) for preconception counselling if she has a current or past severe mental health problem and is planning a pregnancy.

population: Inclusion: women aged 16-45 with a current or past severe mental health problem (psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe depression) under mental health services who document they are planning a pregnancy. Exclusion: women already pregnant at first mention (covered by antenatal pathways instead).
sample: All identified cases in the last 12 months from mental health service records (typically 15-30 women across a community mental health team caseload)
data_source: Community mental health team and perinatal mental health service electronic records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory prompt to the community mental health team electronic care plan review: 'planning a pregnancy: yes/no', which triggers an automatic preconception counselling referral suggestion when answered yes
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the perinatal mental health network governance meeting; if effective, embed the mandatory prompt trust-wide
evidence: [3337] Audit of perinatal assessment documentation found gaps in basic recording during initial assessment in a community perinatal mental health service, showing documentation quality in this pathway is an established but incompletely audited concern
[6309] Audit of GP referrals to perinatal mental health services during a period of service austerity, showing referral pathway quality is a recognised but under-audited issue
pitfalls: Pregnancy planning may be discussed informally in a routine appointment without a specific documented field: agree with clinicians to actively ask and record this at every relevant review
Women may not disclose pregnancy plans to a mental health worker they see infrequently: report the number of women asked as well as the number referred
Specialist perinatal services may have geographic or capacity limits, making referral to a generic secondary service the only option: record this as a partial pass with the reason given
Retrospective identification of 'planning a pregnancy' entries may be difficult if not coded: consider prospective data collection over a fixed window instead of retrospective search
The record may show a referral made but never actioned by the receiving service: check the perinatal team's own referral log for confirmation, not just the sending note
pearls: Recruit the perinatal mental health service lead as a joint audit lead with the adult community mental health team
Use a structured yes/no prompt rather than free text so future searches are reliable
Agree a simple referral pathway and response time standard with the perinatal service before starting, so the change has somewhere to route referrals
Present the finding to the trust's perinatal mental health network (many now exist under the NHS Long Term Plan), which can support scaling the change
Keep prospective data collection running via the new prompt so the re-audit is a simple data pull rather than a fresh manual search
effort: ~20 min per identified case from the mental health electronic record
pass: A referral for preconception counselling is documented as made, or offered and declined, when a woman with a current or past severe mental health problem states she is planning a pregnancy

question: Do women with sudden onset of symptoms suggesting postpartum psychosis have a documented referral to a secondary mental health service (preferably specialist perinatal) with assessment completed within 4 hours of referral?
why: No audit in the library measures the 4-hour assessment standard for suspected postpartum psychosis; this is a specific, time-critical, high-harm NICE recommendation that has not yet been audited in the corpus.

standard.source: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health, rec 1.5.12 (2014)
standard.wording: If a woman has sudden onset of symptoms suggesting postpartum psychosis, refer her to a secondary mental health service (preferably a specialist perinatal mental health service) for immediate assessment (within 4 hours of referral).

population: Inclusion: women referred urgently to mental health services in the postnatal period (within 12 months of delivery) with suspected postpartum psychosis. Exclusion: routine (non-urgent) postnatal mental health referrals.
sample: All identified urgent postpartum psychosis referrals in the last 12 months (typically a small number, 10-20 cases, given the rarity of the presentation; extend the window if fewer than 10 are found)
data_source: Mental health crisis team/perinatal mental health service referral and assessment records

options: managed at home with crisis team

timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'suspected postpartum psychosis' flag to the crisis team referral triage system, which starts a 4-hour countdown timer and pages the on-call perinatal or general psychiatry consultant automatically
reaudit: At 12 months, same template, widened data collection window if numbers remain small
close_loop: Present at the perinatal mental health network and crisis team governance meeting; if effective, embed the flag and countdown timer permanently
evidence: [3337] Audit of perinatal assessment documentation in a community perinatal mental health service found gaps in basic recording, indicating documentation and timeliness of perinatal assessments is an area needing closer measurement
No audit specific to the 4-hour postpartum psychosis assessment standard exists in the library
pitfalls: Postpartum psychosis is rare, so numbers will be very small: report raw numerators/denominators and consider a rolling collection over 12-24 months rather than a single 3-month window
Out-of-hours referrals may go through a different crisis pathway with less clear time-stamping: check both in-hours and out-of-hours logs

A woman may present to a general adult crisis team unfamiliar with the postpartum psychosis red flags and be triaged as routine: check for missed or delayed recognition, not just delay after correct triage
Referral and assessment times may be recorded inconsistently (referral received vs. referral accepted): agree a single time-stamp definition before starting
A perinatal mental health service may not operate 24/7 in smaller areas, meaning the target route is unavailable out of hours: record and report this system gap
pearls: Work with the crisis team and perinatal mental health service together, since the referral usually crosses between them
Use the rarity of the condition as an argument for prospective, continuous data collection via the new flag, rather than a fixed 3-month audit window
Base the change on a simple, recognisable red-flag checklist for postpartum psychosis so referrers do not need specialist perinatal knowledge
Present any near-miss or delayed case (even outside the identified events) as a case study to strengthen the argument for the timer system
Escalate any finding that the specialist perinatal service is unavailable out-of-hours to commissioners, as this is a systemic, not just documentation, gap
effort: ~30 min per identified case from the crisis/perinatal team referral and assessment record
pass: Assessment by a secondary mental health service is documented as completed within 4 hours of the referral being made

question: What proportion of women who may need to take psychotropic medication in pregnancy or the postnatal period have a documented discussion of the benefits of breastfeeding and the risks of the specific medication with breastfeeding?
why: No audit in the library measures this specific breastfeeding and medication discussion, which is distinct from general medication counselling audits already in the corpus.

standard.source: NICE CG192 Antenatal and postnatal mental health, rec 1.4.4 (2014)
standard.wording: Discuss breastfeeding with all women who may need to take psychotropic medication in pregnancy or in the postnatal period. Explain to them the benefits of breastfeeding, the potential risks associated with taking psychotropic medication while breastfeeding...

population: Inclusion: women under perinatal or maternal mental health services prescribed a psychotropic medication in pregnancy or within 12 months postnatally. Exclusion: women who are not breastfeeding and have documented no intention to breastfeed.
sample: 30 consecutive women under perinatal mental health services prescribed a psychotropic medication in the last 12 months
data_source: Perinatal mental health service electronic record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'breastfeeding and medication discussed' checkbox with a free-text summary field to the perinatal mental health medication review template
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the perinatal mental health service governance meeting; if effective, embed the mandatory field permanently
evidence: [3337] Audit of perinatal assessment documentation found basic recording gaps at initial assessment in a community perinatal mental health service, the nearest related entry in the library to structured perinatal discussion documentation
pitfalls: A discussion may happen verbally without being recorded: agree with the team that this is a documentation standard, and undocumented discussions still count as a fail
Specialist perinatal pharmacy advice (e.g. from UKTIS or a specialist pharmacist) may be sought but not linked in the main note: check pharmacy correspondence as well as the clinical note
Women who are not breastfeeding and have no plans to should be excluded, but this needs to be explicitly documented, not assumed
The discussion needs to be specific to the medication prescribed, not a generic breastfeeding leaflet: define this distinction in the data tool
Views may change over the postnatal period (a woman may start breastfeeding after initially not planning to): capture the date of the woman's current status alongside the discussion date
pearls: Recruit the perinatal mental health pharmacist to help build and monitor the mandatory field
Use an established resource (such as a specialist medicines-in-pregnancy/breastfeeding information service) as the reference point for what a 'complete' discussion covers
Present the change as reducing legal and clinical risk from undocumented advice, which helps secure clinical engagement
Time the re-audit for 6 months to capture a full cohort of women moving through pregnancy to the postnatal period
Keep a simple log of specialist pharmacy queries made, as this is a useful secondary marker that the discussion is happening
effort: ~15 min per 10 records from the perinatal mental health record
pass: A dated note records that breastfeeding and the specific medication's risks/benefits were discussed with the woman

question: What proportion of patients in seclusion have a nursing review recorded at least every 2 hours, undertaken by two registered nurses, at least one of whom was not involved in the decision to seclude?
why: The seclusion practice and review topic card in the library (16 audits) shows medical review timing is well studied, but the consultant advice specifically flags out-of-hours timing and independent review as the more useful, currently under-measured angle; nursing review frequency itself is not isolated as its own audit in the corpus.

standard.source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 26.134
standard.wording: Nursing reviews of the secluded patient should take place at least every two hours following the commencement of seclusion. These should be undertaken by two individuals who are registered nurses, and at least one of whom should not have been involved directly in the decision to seclude.

population: Inclusion: all seclusion episodes on adult acute or secure/forensic wards in the audit period lasting 2 hours or more. Exclusion: episodes lasting under 2 hours (no review due).
sample: All seclusion episodes of 2 hours or more in the last 3 months (typically 20-40 episodes across a secure or acute inpatient service)
data_source: Seclusion record/observation chart and incident reporting system
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory seclusion nursing review proforma with a built-in 2-hourly timer and a field confirming the second reviewer's independence, replacing free-text observation entries
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the ward or secure service clinical governance meeting; if effective, adopt the proforma trust-wide across all wards using seclusion
evidence: Topic card 'Seclusion practice and review': medical review within 1 hour is poor at 20-44% across several audits [3273][3188][3281][3459][3380]; a seclusion review template plus teaching achieved 95-100% compliance [3128], and an integrated care pathway raised compliance from 3-100% to 69-100% [3040]
pitfalls: Nursing reviews may be recorded in general nursing notes rather than a dedicated seclusion record, making them hard to find: search both sources
The 'independence' requirement may be poorly understood by staff: provide clear guidance on what counts as involvement in the original decision
Overnight and asleep-patient reviews may follow a modified schedule under local policy: record these separately rather than counting them as missed reviews
A template alone gave only modest gains in one service (75% to 83%) with minimal further change on a statistical process control chart [3552]: plan for ongoing monitoring, not a single fix
Staff may see 2-hourly review as excessive during long seclusion episodes: reinforce the safeguarding rationale in training, not just the form
pearls: Base the proforma directly on Mental Health Act Code of Practice paragraph 26.134 wording so staff can see exactly what is required
Use a physical or electronic timer/alert to prompt the 2-hourly review, since the corpus shows structural prompts outperform teaching alone
Recruit a senior ward nurse as the audit lead, since they can identify realistic barriers to documenting independence
Present the topic card's finding that huddles and weekly meetings raised consultant review compliance from under 70% to over 90% [3105], to support a similar nursing huddle model
Track average seclusion duration alongside review compliance, since the corpus shows a huddle model also reduced average seclusion time from 30 to 20 hours [3105]
effort: ~10 min per seclusion episode from the seclusion record
pass: Every 2-hour interval of the seclusion episode has a nursing review recorded by two registered nurses, with at least one independent of the original decision to seclude

question: Where a patient has been secluded for 8 hours continuously or 12 hours intermittently within a 48-hour period, is an independent multidisciplinary team review carried out promptly, including a doctor, a nurse and other professionals not involved in the incident?
why: The seclusion topic card's consultant advice specifically identifies independent Approved Clinician/MDT review as an under-measured area, distinct from the routine medical and nursing reviews already well audited in the corpus.

standard.source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 26.141
standard.wording: An independent MDT review should be promptly undertaken where a patient has either been secluded for eight hours consecutively or for 12 hours intermittently during a 48-hour period.

population: Inclusion: all seclusion episodes reaching 8 hours continuous or 12 hours intermittent within 48 hours in the audit period. Exclusion: shorter episodes not reaching this trigger.
sample: All qualifying episodes in the last 6 months (numbers will be small in most services; extend the window if fewer than 10 are found)
data_source: Seclusion record and independent MDT review minutes
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic alert to the seclusion record that fires at the 8-hour continuous or 12-hour intermittent trigger, notifying the site manager to convene the independent MDT review
reaudit: At 6 months, same template, widened window if numbers remain small
close_loop: Present at the trust-wide Mental Health Act or restrictive practice governance meeting; if effective, embed the automatic alert across all wards using seclusion
evidence: Topic card 'Seclusion practice and review' notes independent reviews by an Approved Clinician are often missing [3256]; consultant advice specifically names Approved Clinician independent review as a more useful audit focus than repeating medical review timing
pitfalls: Long or intermittent seclusion episodes reaching the 12-hour-in-48-hours trigger may be harder to track than continuous episodes: build a running total into the seclusion record, not a manual calculation
'Independent' membership may be compromised if the same small on-call team covers both the original decision and the review: record and flag this explicitly
IMHA involvement may not be arranged in time, especially out of hours: track whether the patient has an IMHA and whether they were invited
Numbers will be small: consider extending data collection to 6-12 months and pooling with other wards in the same secure service if needed
A review that happens late may still be recorded as 'done' without the delay being visible: always capture the time from trigger to review, not just yes/no
pearls: Build the 8-hour/12-hour trigger calculation into the seclusion record software so staff do not need to calculate it manually
Involve the trust's Mental Health Act administrator, who is well placed to track prolonged seclusion episodes across wards
Use this audit to also check IMHA involvement, since the two safeguards are meant to work together
Present near-miss cases (episodes close to but not reaching the trigger) to show the alert would have helped, even with a small confirmed sample
Since this trigger is rare, keep it as a standing, continuously monitored indicator rather than a one-off audit
effort: ~20 min per qualifying episode from the seclusion record and MDT minutes
pass: An independent MDT review, with the required minimum membership and none of them involved in the original seclusion decision, is documented as carried out on reaching the 8-hour/12-hour trigger

question: Does the seclusion care plan for every patient in seclusion include, as a minimum, a statement of clinical needs and risks, a plan for meeting needs and de-escalation, and details of bedding, clothing and dietary provision, as required by the Mental Health Act Code of Practice?
why: No audit in the library checks the specific minimum content of a seclusion care plan as set out in the Code of Practice; existing seclusion audits in the corpus focus on review timing, not care plan content.

standard.source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 26.147
standard.wording: As a minimum the seclusion care plan should include: a statement of clinical needs (including any physical or mental health problems), risks and treatment objectives; a plan as to how needs are to be met, how de-escalation attempts will continue and how risks will be managed; details of bedding and clothing to be provided; details as to how the patient's dietary needs are to be provided for.

population: Inclusion: all seclusion episodes lasting more than 2 hours in the audit period. Exclusion: very brief episodes ended before a care plan would normally be completed.
sample: All seclusion episodes over 2 hours in the last 3 months (typically 20-40 episodes)
data_source: Seclusion care plan documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Replace the free-text seclusion care plan section with a structured proforma with the four mandatory headings from the Code of Practice, so none can be skipped
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the ward or secure service clinical governance meeting; if effective, adopt the structured proforma trust-wide
evidence: Topic card 'Seclusion practice and review': content gaps in seclusion reviews include medication side effects documented in 0% [3627] and risk to self in 5% [3380] of reviews, and no review met all eight assessed criteria in one audit [3627], showing structured content (not just timing) is a known weak point
pitfalls: Staff may complete a generic care plan template not specific to seclusion, missing the required elements: check against the exact four headings, not a general impression of completeness
Bedding/clothing and dietary needs may be managed verbally by nursing staff without being written into the plan: this should still count as a fail, since the standard requires documentation
Care plans may be updated as seclusion continues, so audit the most recent version, but also check the plan was in place from early in the episode, not only by the time it ended
A well-intentioned but generic 'as per care plan' note without specific content should not count as a pass
Fatigue during very long seclusion episodes may mean updates lapse over time: sample from both early and later points in longer episodes if resources allow
pearls: Base the structured proforma exactly on Code of Practice paragraph 26.147 so nothing required is left to interpretation
Recruit ward matrons/senior nurses to pilot the new proforma before a full rollout, since they complete these plans in practice
Link this audit with the seclusion review audits (nursing/medical/independent) so a single data collection exercise can gather several linked measures
Share examples of complete versus incomplete plans anonymised from the audit findings, to help staff see what 'good' looks like
Keep the proforma under the ward's own clinical documentation folder so it survives staff rotation
effort: ~10 min per episode from the seclusion care plan record
pass: All four minimum elements (clinical needs/risks, de-escalation plan, bedding/clothing, dietary needs) are present in the seclusion care plan

question: Before section 17 leave is first granted to a detained patient, is a documented risk assessment carried out and any necessary safeguards put in place, as required by the Mental Health Act Code of Practice?
why: An existing library audit found no updated risk assessment before leave in 83% of cases at one old age psychiatric ward [3245], but no audit in the library has since tested whether a mandatory risk assessment step closes this specific gap.

standard.source: Mental Health Act 1983 Code of Practice (2015), paragraph 27.10
standard.wording: When considering and planning leave of absence, responsible clinicians should: ... undertake a risk assessment and put in place any necessary safeguards ...

population: Inclusion: all detained patients newly granted section 17 leave for the first time in the audit period. Exclusion: routine ward-based leave that does not require a section 17 form (e.g. informal patients).
sample: 30 consecutive first-time section 17 leave authorisations in the last 3 months, across acute and secure/forensic wards
data_source: Section 17 leave form and risk assessment documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory risk assessment field to the electronic section 17 leave form, which cannot be submitted for signature without a completed, dated risk assessment attached
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the Mental Health Act or ward clinical governance meeting; if effective, adopt the mandatory field trust-wide
evidence: [3245] Application of Section 17 Leave on an old age psychiatric ward found no updated risk assessment before leave in 83% of cases (5/6) and no S17 form uploaded in 25%
[3505] Section 17 Leave Utilisation and Outcomes in Acute Adult Psychiatric Inpatients: a closed-loop audit, showing this topic is auditable and re-auditable in the corpus
[7449] National audit of NHS mental health leave policies found domain consistency as low as 41.9% for types of leave, showing local policy variation is a known contributing factor
pitfalls: A generic ward risk assessment done on admission may be wrongly counted as the leave-specific risk assessment: require it to be dated at or after the leave decision and to reference the leave itself
Escorted vs unescorted leave carry different risk profiles: record which type of leave was granted, since a blanket risk assessment may not address both
For patients on long-term leave with periodic short extensions, distinguish the first grant (audited here) from routine extensions
Forensic/secure wards may already do this well due to existing MDT risk review processes: report results by ward type to identify where the gap is greatest
A documented risk assessment that is a copy-paste from a previous one without genuine reassessment should not count as a pass
pearls: Use the existing library audit [3245] baseline (83% missing) as the starting comparison point to show the scale of the problem
Recruit the Mental Health Act administrator, who processes every section 17 form, to help identify the sample and enforce the mandatory field
Agree with ward consultants in advance what counts as an adequate risk assessment specific to leave (not just a general admission risk assessment)
Present the [3505] closed-loop audit's approach as a template for how to structure the re-audit
Fix ownership of the audit with the Mental Health Act office, which has continuous oversight of every section 17 form issued
effort: ~15 min per authorisation from the section 17 form and risk assessment record
pass: A documented risk assessment, dated before or on the date leave is first authorised, is present with any safeguards specified

question: In secure or smoke-free mental health units, do patients taking clozapine or olanzapine who stop or significantly reduce smoking have a documented dose review or plasma level check within 1 week of the change in smoking status?
why: Secure units and prisons are smoke-free environments, creating a sudden change in smoking status for patients on clozapine; no audit in the library links this specific, high-harm interaction (smoking cessation raising clozapine levels through reduced enzyme induction) to a documented monitoring response, despite the general clozapine monitoring topic card (8 audits) covering routine blood monitoring only.

standard.source: NICE CG178 Psychosis and schizophrenia in adults: prevention and management, rec 1.1.2.3 (2014)
standard.wording: Offer people with psychosis or schizophrenia who smoke help to stop smoking, even if previous attempts have been unsuccessful. Be aware of the potential significant impact of reducing cigarette smoking on the metabolism of other drugs, particularly clozapine and olanzapine.

population: Inclusion: patients in a secure or smoke-free mental health unit on clozapine or olanzapine who have a documented reduction or cessation of smoking in the audit period. Exclusion: patients who were already non-smokers before admission.
sample: All identified cases of smoking reduction/cessation on clozapine or olanzapine in the last 12 months across the secure service (numbers will vary; expect roughly 10-25 cases given typical smoke-free unit admission rates)
data_source: Secure unit electronic prescribing record, smoking cessation service records and clozapine monitoring log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic alert to the electronic prescribing record that fires when a patient on clozapine or olanzapine is flagged as reducing or stopping smoking (via the smoking cessation service record), prompting an urgent dose review and plasma level request
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the secure service pharmacy and medicines safety governance meeting; if effective, embed the automatic alert across all smoke-free mental health units
evidence: Topic card 'Clozapine monitoring' (8 audits): FBC monitoring is consistently near 100% [3226][3386][3465], but cardiovascular and initiation-related monitoring (troponin, CRP) is poor, and no audit in the corpus covers the smoking-cessation dose interaction specifically, despite this being a well-recognised safety issue in smoke-free secure settings
pitfalls: Smoking status changes may not be formally recorded outside the smoking cessation service, especially if a patient simply cannot smoke on a secure ward without a documented cessation attempt: cross-check ward observation notes as well
