A patient may relapse and restart smoking during a leave period, requiring the reverse adjustment: track both directions of change, not just cessation
Some units may already build in an automatic clozapine level check on admission to a smoke-free ward regardless of prior smoking status: record baseline unit practice before assuming a gap exists
Toxicity symptoms (sedation, hypersalivation, seizures) may be misattributed to other causes: prompt staff to consider the smoking-clozapine interaction explicitly in the proforma
Numbers will be small in a single unit: consider pooling data across a regional secure services network
pearls: Involve the secure unit's pharmacist and smoking cessation lead jointly, since this crosses both services
Use national forensic pharmacy network guidance (where available) alongside the CG178 recommendation to design the alert threshold
Present real (anonymised) cases of clozapine toxicity linked to smoking cessation from national safety alerts to support the case for change
Build the alert to also flag e-cigarette or vaping changes, since nicotine (not smoke) is not the enzyme-inducing component, and confusion here is common
Keep monitoring live rather than a single cycle, since a secure ward's smoke-free policy affects every new admission who smokes
effort: ~20 min per identified case from the prescribing and smoking cessation record
pass: A dose review (with or without a change) or a clozapine plasma level check is documented within 1 week of a recorded reduction or stop in smoking

question: What proportion of patients with an eating disorder admitted to a medical or paediatric ward have a physical risk assessment that includes nutritional status, disordered eating behaviours, physical examination, blood tests and electrocardiography, as recommended by MEED?
why: No audit in the library measures compliance with the MEED (Medical Emergencies in Eating Disorders) risk assessment framework at the point of medical admission, despite this being the central recommendation of RCPsych CR233 and a recognised high-harm gap (patients can appear well with normal bloods yet be at high risk).

standard.source: Royal College of Psychiatrists CR233 Medical emergencies in eating disorders: guidance on recognition and management, recommendation 3 (2022)
standard.wording: Physical risk assessment in primary and secondary settings should include nutritional status (including current intake), disordered eating behaviours, physical examination, blood tests and electrocardiography.

population: Inclusion: patients of any age admitted to a medical, paediatric or psychiatric ward with a known or suspected eating disorder. Exclusion: patients admitted for an unrelated acute condition with an incidental historical eating disorder diagnosis not currently active.
sample: 30 consecutive eating disorder-related medical/paediatric admissions over the last 6 months
data_source: Medical/paediatric admission clerking and nursing assessment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Introduce a MEED-based eating disorder admission proforma with all five elements as mandatory fields, triggered automatically by an eating disorder diagnosis code or referral
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the joint medical/paediatric and eating disorder service governance meeting; if effective, embed the proforma as the standard admission document
evidence: Related entries in the library concern eating disorder physical risk monitoring in community CAMHS [3306] and day-care settings [3340], which show monitoring completeness varies widely (e.g. temperature recorded in only 5-30% of cases [3306]), but no audit yet targets the specific MEED admission risk assessment bundle on a medical or paediatric ward
pitfalls: Medical and paediatric teams unfamiliar with MEED may not recognise the need for the full bundle if the patient appears clinically well: include awareness training alongside the proforma
ECG may be delayed or deferred if the patient is thought to be 'medically stable': define the audit standard as within 24 hours regardless of apparent stability
Disordered eating behaviours may be under-documented due to patient reluctance to disclose: record what was asked, not just what was found
A generic 'bloods taken' entry without specifying which tests (including phosphate, magnesium) may overstate compliance: specify the required panel in the data tool
Small numbers in a single hospital: consider pooling data across a regional eating disorder network if fewer than 20 cases are found in 6 months
pearls: Base the proforma on the CR233 summary sheets (Annexe 1), which are designed as quick-reference guides for non-specialist medical and paediatric staff
Involve the eating disorder service's specialist dietitian and physician in designing the proforma so it fits real ward workflow
Present the CR233 finding that patients can appear well with normal bloods but still be high risk, to build buy-in from medical/paediatric teams who may otherwise underestimate risk
Link the proforma trigger to the eating disorder referral or diagnosis code so it activates automatically rather than relying on staff to remember
Share results with both the medical/paediatric directorate and the eating disorder service, since both need to act on gaps
effort: ~20 min per 10 admissions from the clerking record
pass: All five elements (nutritional status, disordered eating behaviours, physical examination, blood tests, ECG) are recorded within 24 hours of admission

question: What proportion of patients under 18 admitted with an eating disorder have their physical risk assessed using age-adjusted thresholds for BMI and blood pressure, rather than adult reference ranges?
why: No audit in the library checks whether age-adjusted (centile-based) thresholds are used for under-18s with eating disorders, despite MEED explicitly requiring this and adult thresholds being known to underestimate risk in children and adolescents.

standard.source: Royal College of Psychiatrists CR233 Medical emergencies in eating disorders: guidance on recognition and management, recommendation 4 (2022)
standard.wording: Assessment measures (such as body mass index [BMI] or blood pressure [BP]) for patients under 18 years must be age-adjusted.

population: Inclusion: patients aged under 18 admitted to a paediatric or CAMHS eating disorder service. Exclusion: patients admitted primarily for another condition with an eating disorder as an incidental past history.
sample: 30 consecutive under-18 eating disorder admissions over the last 12 months
data_source: Paediatric/CAMHS eating disorder admission and risk assessment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Build an automatic BMI centile and age-adjusted blood pressure calculator into the paediatric eating disorder admission proforma, replacing free-text adult BMI entry
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the CAMHS/paediatric eating disorder service governance meeting; if effective, embed the calculator permanently
evidence: [3306] Assessment and management of eating disorders at community CAMHS found variable recording of key physical parameters (weight change 40%, temperature 5%), showing physical risk documentation in CAMHS eating disorder services is an established but incompletely closed gap
pitfalls: Staff trained primarily in adult eating disorder services may default to adult BMI thresholds out of habit: highlight this explicitly in training
A centile chart may be available on paper but not transferred into the electronic record: check both sources
Growth faltering in younger adolescents can be missed if only a single BMI centile is checked rather than trend over time: consider capturing a growth trajectory as a secondary measure
Some electronic systems may not support automatic centile calculation, requiring a manual chart: budget for this if an IT fix is not immediately available
Transitional-age patients (17-18) moving between CAMHS and adult services may have inconsistent practice: flag these cases separately
pearls: Use the RCPCH UK-WHO growth charts (or trust-approved equivalent) as the reference standard for age-adjustment
Involve a paediatrician or paediatric dietitian in building the calculator to ensure clinical accuracy
Present the CR233 rationale (adult thresholds underestimate risk in the young) directly to staff to explain why this matters
Pilot the automatic calculator with one admitting team before wider rollout to catch usability issues
Align the re-audit with the CAMHS eating disorder service's existing annual quality review cycle
effort: ~15 min per 10 admissions from the paediatric/CAMHS record
pass: BMI is recorded as a centile or percentage of median BMI for age, and blood pressure is compared against an age-adjusted (not adult) reference range

question: What proportion of patients identified as high risk of refeeding syndrome on eating disorder admission receive thiamine before enteral or oral refeeding begins?
why: No audit in the library applies the MEED refeeding risk framework specifically to eating disorder admissions; a related general refeeding audit exists for enteral/parenteral nutrition patients generally, but not one grounded in MEED's eating-disorder-specific risk criteria.

standard.source: Royal College of Psychiatrists CR233 Medical emergencies in eating disorders: guidance on recognition and management, section 4 Safe refeeding of malnourished patients with restrictive eating disorders (2022)
standard.wording: avoid refeeding syndrome caused by too rapid refeeding ... safely refeed the patient

population: Inclusion: patients admitted with a restrictive eating disorder identified as high risk of refeeding syndrome (using MEED criteria such as very low BMI, minimal recent intake, or rapid weight loss). Exclusion: patients assessed as low risk of refeeding syndrome.
sample: 20-30 consecutive high-refeeding-risk eating disorder admissions over the last 12 months (a longer window may be needed given lower admission volumes for this specific risk group)
data_source: Eating disorder/medical admission drug chart and dietitian assessment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a MEED-based refeeding risk grid to the eating disorder admission and drug chart, which pre-selects thiamine on the drug chart automatically when high risk is ticked
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the eating disorder service and pharmacy governance meeting; if effective, embed the pre-selected order set permanently
evidence: No audit in the library applies the MEED-specific refeeding risk framework to eating disorder admissions; the nearest related entry, a general refeeding audit for enteral/parenteral nutrition patients using NICE CG32, shows a comparable gap exists in the general medical population
pitfalls: Eating disorder patients may start oral intake gradually without a formal 'refeeding start' order, making the index time unclear: define the start point as the first recorded increase in calorie intake
Risk grading may be done informally by the dietitian without a documented score: require the MEED risk grid to be completed and filed
Community/day-care patients starting a structured meal plan at home are harder to audit than inpatients: restrict this cycle to inpatient admissions only
Thiamine given after feeding has already started should count as a fail even if given the same day: capture the exact timing relative to the first feed
A patient may already be on oral thiamine from a GP for unrelated reasons: check that the dose and timing meet the refeeding-specific protocol, not just any thiamine prescription
pearls: Use the MEED refeeding decision tree (CR233 Figure 4) directly as the basis for the risk grid
Involve the eating disorder service dietitian, who typically leads on refeeding risk grading, as a joint audit lead
Present the audit alongside the existing general refeeding syndrome audit findings in the corpus to show the gap is consistent across settings
Build the thiamine pre-selection into the electronic drug chart order set so the fix does not depend on staff memory
Track any refeeding syndrome events (electrolyte derangement) alongside compliance, to show clinical impact at re-audit
effort: ~20 min per admission from the drug chart and dietitian record
pass: Thiamine (oral or intravenous, per local protocol) is given before or at the start of refeeding for every patient identified as high risk using the MEED risk factors for refeeding

question: What proportion of patients with an eating disorder taking medication that could compromise cardiac function (including medication that could cause electrolyte imbalance, bradycardia below 40 beats per minute, hypokalaemia, or a prolonged QT interval) are offered ECG monitoring?
why: No audit in the library links eating disorder medication choice to the specific NICE-recommended ECG monitoring requirement; existing eating disorder physical monitoring audits in the corpus measure general ECG completion rates, not this medication-triggered indication.

standard.source: NICE NG69 Eating disorders: recognition and treatment, rec 1.8.17 (2017)
standard.wording: Offer electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring for people with an eating disorder who are taking medication that could compromise cardiac functioning (including medication that could cause electrolyte imbalance, bradycardia below 40 beats per minute, hypokalaemia, or a prolonged QT interval).

population: Inclusion: patients with an active eating disorder prescribed a medication with a known cardiac risk (e.g. certain antipsychotics, some antidepressants, stimulant laxatives affecting potassium). Exclusion: patients on no such medication.
sample: 30 consecutive patients with an active eating disorder on a cardiac-risk medication, identified from the eating disorder service caseload over the last 12 months
data_source: Eating disorder service electronic record and ECG department log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic ECG-offer prompt to the eating disorder service e-prescribing system, triggered whenever a medication on a defined cardiac-risk list is prescribed to a patient with an active eating disorder
reaudit: At 12 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the eating disorder service and pharmacy governance meeting; if effective, embed the automatic prompt permanently
evidence: [3340] Re-audit of physical health monitoring of day-care eating disorder patients found ECG and bloods fell by 11.1% at all monitoring points despite good BMI/BP/pulse compliance, showing ECG specifically is the weaker element even where general monitoring improves
[3306] Community CAMHS eating disorder audit found ECG recording at 75% in cycle 1, falling to 40% in cycle 2, showing this measure can worsen without a structural fix
pitfalls: The defined list of 'cardiac-risk medications' needs pharmacy input, since risk varies by dose and individual patient factors: agree this list before data collection
Patients may decline ECG monitoring, especially if needle- or procedure-anxious: record declines as a distinct category rather than a system failure
A historical ECG from before the medication was started should not count as current monitoring: require the ECG to be after the medication was started or at a defined interval
The corpus shows ECG completion can fall between cycles even after a documented improvement: build monitoring into a permanent system change, not a one-off intervention
Community and day-care patients may need to travel for ECG access, creating a practical barrier: consider community ECG provision as part of the change
pearls: Agree the specific cardiac-risk medication list with eating disorder pharmacy and cardiology input before starting
Use the corpus finding that ECG/bloods worsened after an initial improvement [3306] to argue for an automatic system prompt rather than a reminder poster
Recruit the eating disorder service's medical lead to champion the change, since they will need to interpret ECG results
Track the reason for any ECG not performed (declined, access issue, clinical decision) so the fix can be targeted correctly
Repeat the audit at 12 months to check the automatic prompt has not faded in effect, as seen elsewhere in the corpus
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from the eating disorder and ECG department records
pass: ECG monitoring is documented as offered (and either accepted and performed, or declined) for every patient on a medication with cardiac risk while an eating disorder is active

question: Does the written record of a mental capacity assessment name the specific decision the person is being asked to make, rather than a general statement that the person 'lacks capacity'?
why: The mental capacity assessment documentation topic card in the library (5 audits) shows the specific decision is named in only 37% of cases [3641]; the consultant advice specifically recommends auditing whether the decision is specific, which this audit targets directly rather than repeating whether a capacity assessment exists at all.

standard.source: NICE NG108 Decision-making and mental capacity, rec 1.1.28 (2018)
standard.wording: Practitioners should make a written record of the decision-making process, which is proportionate to the decision being made. ... Include: what the person is being asked to decide ... whether on the balance of probabilities a person lacks capacity to make a decision.

population: Inclusion: liaison psychiatry mental capacity assessments carried out on general medical, surgical or emergency department patients in the audit period. Exclusion: capacity assessments carried out solely under the Mental Health Act for treatment refusal already covered by other legislation.
sample: 30 consecutive liaison psychiatry mental capacity assessments over the last 3 months
data_source: Liaison psychiatry electronic record and mental capacity assessment proforma
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Replace the free-text capacity assessment note with a structured proforma that requires the specific decision to be typed into a mandatory field before the assessment can be saved
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the liaison psychiatry governance meeting; if effective, embed the structured proforma trust-wide for all capacity assessments
evidence: Topic card 'Mental capacity assessment documentation': the specific decision is named in only 37% of assessments [3641]; a 30-minute teaching session on a structured MCA template raised the diagnostic test element from 77.5% to 95% and functional test parts from 70% to 90-100% [3531]
pitfalls: Clinicians may write 'capacity for discharge' as a decision when the actual decision is narrower (e.g. capacity to consent to a specific treatment): define 'specific' clearly in the data tool with examples
Multiple decisions may be assessed in one encounter (e.g. treatment and discharge): record each decision separately rather than as one combined entry
A well-completed proforma from one liaison clinician does not guarantee trust-wide uptake: monitor variation between individual assessors, not just an overall average
The MCA teaching intervention in the corpus [3531] was not stated to have been re-audited beyond the immediate cycle: build in the mandatory field so gains are not teaching-dependent
Time pressure in acute settings may lead to brief, non-specific entries: consider a very short mandatory field rather than a lengthy form to protect completion rates
pearls: Base the mandatory field wording directly on NG108 1.1.28 so there is no ambiguity about what 'specific' means
Recruit the liaison psychiatry service's own quality lead to pilot the proforma before wider rollout
Use the corpus finding that teaching alone raised compliance from 77.5% to 95% [3531] to show the size of gain possible, then aim to lock this in structurally
Present anonymised examples of vague versus specific decision statements in a short teaching session alongside the proforma launch
Track completion by individual assessor at re-audit to identify anyone needing extra support, without naming individuals in the wider report
effort: ~10 min per 10 records from the liaison psychiatry proforma
pass: The record states the specific decision in question (e.g. 'to consent to insertion of a nasogastric tube', not just 'capacity') and a specific conclusion about capacity for that decision

question: Does the written record of a mental capacity assessment include the reasoning for the conclusion under each of the four functional test elements (understand, retain, weigh up, communicate), rather than a bare conclusion?
why: The mental capacity assessment topic card's consultant advice highlights that functional tests lack evidence in 40-50% of assessments [3641] and recommends auditing the quality of the four functional tests rather than repeating whether a capacity assessment exists.

standard.source: NICE NG108 Decision-making and mental capacity, rec 1.1.28 (2018)
standard.wording: Practitioners should make a written record of the decision-making process... Include: ... steps taken to help the person make the decision ... key considerations for the person in making the decision ... needs identified as a result of the decision.

population: Inclusion: liaison psychiatry mental capacity assessments concluding the person lacks capacity for a specific decision, carried out in the audit period. Exclusion: assessments concluding the person has capacity, where the standard of detail required differs.
sample: 30 consecutive liaison psychiatry mental capacity assessments concluding a lack of capacity, over the last 6 months
data_source: Liaison psychiatry electronic record and mental capacity assessment proforma
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add four mandatory free-text boxes to the capacity proforma, one per functional test element, each requiring a specific entry (not a repeated tick) before the assessment can be saved
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the liaison psychiatry governance meeting; if effective, embed the four-box structure trust-wide
evidence: Topic card 'Mental capacity assessment documentation': functional tests lack evidence in 40-50% of assessments [3641]; a structured MCA template with teaching raised the functional test elements from 70% to 90-100% [3531]
pitfalls: Clinicians experienced in capacity assessment may feel a four-box structure is unnecessarily rigid for a clear-cut case: pilot with a senior clinician first to refine wording
A single sentence covering all four elements together may be entered into one box: require each box to be completed individually
Assessments done jointly with another specialty (e.g. surgery) may be recorded in a different note format outside liaison psychiatry's own system: check both sources
Retrospective identification of 'lacks capacity' conclusions may need a coded search: agree the search term with the liaison team's data administrator
A well-completed proforma at initiation does not guarantee ongoing quality: monitor a rolling sample rather than a single cycle only
pearls: Reuse and adapt the structured MCA template already shown to work in the corpus [3531] rather than designing a new one from scratch
Recruit a liaison psychiatry consultant to co-design the four-box wording so it captures genuine clinical reasoning, not just a repeated tick
Present the 40-50% baseline finding from the topic card to secure buy-in for the change
Track whether the quality improvement is sustained six months after the initial teaching seen in [3531], since teaching effects can fade
Keep an example bank of well-reasoned, anonymised entries to use in ongoing induction for new liaison trainees
effort: ~15 min per 10 records from the liaison psychiatry proforma
pass: Evidence or reasoning is recorded for each of the four functional test elements (understanding, retaining, weighing up, communicating the decision), not just a yes/no conclusion

question: What proportion of liaison psychiatry referrals for acute confusion in general hospital inpatients have a 4AT assessment completed before or as part of the liaison assessment?
why: The delirium screening topic card in the library (17 audits) is described as heavily overdone for general ward screening rates; the consultant advice recommends auditing whether a positive 4AT leads to a formal diagnosis, which requires first establishing 4AT use specifically within the liaison psychiatry referral pathway, not yet isolated in the corpus.

standard.source: NICE CG103 Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management in hospital and long-term care, rec 1.6.1 (2010, updated 2023)
standard.wording: If indicators of delirium are identified, a health or social care practitioner who is competent to do so should carry out an assessment using the 4AT tool.

population: Inclusion: liaison psychiatry referrals for acute confusion, agitation or query delirium on general medical/surgical wards (excluding orthopaedic wards, already separately audited in the corpus). Exclusion: referrals for pre-existing dementia with no acute change.
sample: 30 consecutive liaison psychiatry referrals for acute confusion over the last 3 months
data_source: Liaison psychiatry referral and assessment record, cross-checked against ward observation charts
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Make a 4AT score a mandatory field on the liaison psychiatry referral form, which cannot be submitted without either a score or a documented reason it could not be completed
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the liaison psychiatry and general medicine joint governance meeting; if effective, adopt the mandatory referral field trust-wide
evidence: Topic card 'Delirium screening and management' (heavily overdone at ward level, 17 audits): screening rates as low as 2.7% [1806] and 3% [1847]; an electronic notes system with a compulsory switch to 4AT raised screening from 3% to 87% [1847], and a champions group with a 4AT sticker proforma raised it from 0% to 92% [1790]
pitfalls: This audit targets the liaison referral pathway specifically, not general ward screening: exclude referrals where 4AT was clearly not indicated (e.g. clear acute stroke referral) to avoid repeating the overdone ward-level measure
A 4AT may be completed but not communicated to the liaison team at referral: check both the ward chart and the liaison referral form
The library shows gains from stickers and lanyard cards faded over a few weeks [1781][1875][3442]: plan for a mandatory field, not a passive reminder
Referrals made verbally or by phone before a formal written referral may bypass the mandatory field: agree that all referrals must be confirmed in writing with the field completed
Non-orthopaedic wards vary widely in delirium awareness: report results by ward type to target further work
pearls: Frame this specifically as a liaison-referral-pathway audit to avoid duplicating the corpus's already extensive ward-level delirium screening audits
Use the corpus's clear finding that only a compulsory electronic field held gains, to justify a mandatory (not optional) referral field
Recruit the liaison psychiatry team's referral coordinator to monitor and enforce the mandatory field
Present the audit alongside the follow-on diagnosis audit (see the linked liaison audit on final diagnosis) as a two-part quality improvement package
Track whether the referring ward type predicts poor compliance, to target teaching where it is most needed
effort: ~10 min per 10 referrals from the referral and ward observation record
pass: A 4AT score is recorded either by the referring ward before liaison psychiatry assessment, or by the liaison psychiatry team at the point of assessment

question: Where a liaison psychiatry 4AT assessment score is 4 or more (suggesting delirium), is a final diagnosis of delirium confirmed or excluded by a clinician with the relevant expertise, rather than left recorded only as 'query delirium'?
why: The delirium topic card's consultant advice specifically recommends auditing whether a positive 4AT leads to a formal diagnosis and management plan, rather than repeating the well-established finding that ward-level 4AT screening rates are poor.

standard.source: NICE CG103 Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management in hospital and long-term care, rec 1.6.2 (2010, updated 2023)
standard.wording: If the assessment described in recommendation 1.6.1 indicates delirium, a healthcare professional with the relevant expertise should make the final diagnosis. This could be the same person who made the assessment.

population: Inclusion: liaison psychiatry assessments where the 4AT score was 4 or more. Exclusion: 4AT scores under 4 (delirium unlikely).
sample: All liaison psychiatry assessments with a 4AT score of 4 or more in the last 6 months (typically 20-30 cases in a general hospital with an active liaison service)
data_source: Liaison psychiatry assessment record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'final diagnosis' field to the liaison psychiatry assessment template for any 4AT score of 4 or more, which cannot be left as 'query delirium' without an explicit plan to review and confirm within 48 hours
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the liaison psychiatry clinical governance meeting; if effective, embed the mandatory field permanently
evidence: Topic card 'Delirium screening and management': formal diagnosis and management stayed low even where screening improved; antipsychotics were started without a diagnosis in one audit [1870]; bedside CAM-ICU training cut misdiagnosed 'psychosis' from 63% to 31% [1365], showing formal diagnosis (not just screening) is the genuine remaining gap
pitfalls: 'Query delirium' may persist in the notes even after a clear diagnosis is later made verbally: require the final diagnosis to be a discrete, searchable entry
Delirium superimposed on dementia can be genuinely difficult to distinguish: this audit should record 'delirium superimposed on dementia' as a valid, positive answer, not a fail
A patient discharged or transferred before a final diagnosis is reached should be recorded separately, since resolution may happen elsewhere
Antipsychotic prescribing without a documented diagnosis is a red flag identified in the corpus [1870]: capture this as a linked secondary measure
Liaison psychiatry may see the patient only once and rely on the ward team for follow-up: track who is responsible for confirming the diagnosis if not resolved at first assessment
pearls: Pair this audit with the referral-stage 4AT audit above so the full pathway from referral to diagnosis is covered by one data collection exercise
Use the corpus finding on misdiagnosed 'psychosis' [1365] to illustrate the harm of an unresolved 'query delirium' label
Recruit a liaison psychiatry consultant to define what counts as 'relevant expertise' for the final diagnosis in the local service
Track whether an antipsychotic was started without a documented diagnosis, as a secondary safety indicator
Present the two linked audits (referral 4AT and final diagnosis) together to the ward teams so the whole pathway, not just liaison psychiatry, understands its role
effort: ~15 min per identified case from the liaison psychiatry record
pass: A final diagnosis (delirium confirmed, delirium excluded, or delirium superimposed on dementia) is documented by a clinician with relevant expertise, and a management plan follows

question: Where a person's presentation makes it difficult to distinguish between delirium, dementia or delirium superimposed on dementia, is the delirium managed first, as required by NICE, rather than management being deferred pending a definitive diagnosis?
why: No audit in the library specifically tests NICE's explicit instruction to manage delirium first when diagnosis is unclear; existing delirium and dementia audits in the corpus measure screening and diagnosis rates but not this specific management-priority rule.

standard.source: NICE CG103 Delirium: prevention, diagnosis and management in hospital and long-term care, rec 1.6.3 (2010)
standard.wording: If there is difficulty distinguishing between the diagnoses of delirium, dementia or delirium superimposed on dementia, manage the delirium first.

population: Inclusion: liaison psychiatry or general medical assessments where the notes explicitly record diagnostic uncertainty between delirium and dementia. Exclusion: cases with a clear, undisputed diagnosis from the outset.
sample: All identified cases of documented diagnostic uncertainty in the last 6 months (typically 15-25 cases in a general hospital with an active liaison service)
data_source: Liaison psychiatry and general medical/elderly care assessment records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a short delirium management checklist (reversible causes, medication review, environment) directly to the liaison psychiatry proforma, triggered automatically whenever 'diagnostic uncertainty' is selected as an outcome
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample definition
close_loop: Present at the liaison psychiatry and elderly care governance meeting; if effective, embed the automatic checklist trigger permanently
evidence: Topic card 'Delirium screening and management' notes formal diagnosis and management stayed low even where screening improved, and that PINCH-ME risk factor management was documented in only 8.5-28% of cases, showing management action (as opposed to diagnosis alone) is the recognised remaining gap
pitfalls: Diagnostic uncertainty may not be recorded as a discrete, searchable phrase: agree a short list of equivalent phrases (e.g. 'query delirium on dementia', 'difficult to distinguish') with the coding team

Teams may wait for cognitive testing results before starting any management, believing this is safer: reinforce in training that NICE recommends managing delirium first specifically because waiting can cause harm
A delirium management plan may be started informally (e.g. verbally asking to stop a medication) without being documented: this should still count as a fail if not written down
Elderly care and liaison psychiatry may each assume the other team is leading management: clarify ownership in the proforma
Retrospective case-finding for 'uncertainty' will be slower than for a coded diagnosis: budget more time for data collection than for a straightforward yes/no audit
pearls: Use the exact NICE wording ('manage the delirium first') as the standard so there is no room for a 'wait and see' interpretation
Recruit a liaison old age psychiatrist and a geriatrician jointly, since this decision typically sits between the two specialties
Frame training around the harm of delay (worsening delirium, falls, increased length of stay) rather than just the documentation requirement
Build the checklist to be quick to complete (a handful of tick boxes) so it does not become a barrier to fast action
Present real (anonymised) cases where delay caused harm, if available locally, to strengthen buy-in
effort: ~15 min per identified case from the joint liaison/elderly care record
pass: Where the notes record diagnostic uncertainty between delirium and dementia, a delirium management plan (addressing reversible causes, environment, medication review) is started without waiting for a definitive diagnosis

question: What proportion of people newly diagnosed with dementia are given oral and written information at diagnosis explaining their dementia subtype, expected changes, and which professionals will be involved in their care and how to contact them?
why: No audit in the library measures compliance with this specific NICE post-diagnostic information requirement; existing corpus entries on old age psychiatry assessment quality focus on the diagnostic process itself, not what is given to the patient once a diagnosis is made.

standard.source: NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers, rec 1.1.6 (2018)
standard.wording: At diagnosis, offer the person and their family members or carers (as appropriate) oral and written information that explains: what their dementia subtype is and the changes to expect as the condition progresses; which healthcare professionals and social care teams will be involved in their care and how to contact them.

population: Inclusion: adults given a new diagnosis of dementia by an old age psychiatry or memory assessment service in the audit period. Exclusion: diagnoses confirmed by another specialty (e.g. neurology) outside old age psychiatry.
sample: 30 consecutive new dementia diagnoses over the last 6 months, from the memory assessment service or old age psychiatry clinic
data_source: Memory assessment service/old age psychiatry electronic record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Create a standard post-diagnostic information pack (one per dementia subtype) with a named team contact sheet, and make handing it out a mandatory step in the diagnosis appointment template
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the memory assessment service or old age psychiatry governance meeting; if effective, embed the information pack as standard practice
evidence: Related library entries concern old age psychiatry new patient assessment quality and memory service referral quality, but no audit yet checks what information is given once a diagnosis is confirmed
pitfalls: A verbal explanation without a written record of what was said or given should not count as a pass: define this clearly in the data tool
Subtype-specific information (e.g. Lewy body versus Alzheimer's) may not be readily available as separate leaflets: check whether generic information was used and whether this meets the standard
Diagnoses given jointly with a GP or via a letter rather than a face-to-face appointment need a different process for delivering information: record the diagnosis method
Family members may be given the information while the patient with reduced capacity is not directly addressed: record who received the information
Contact information may go out of date if staff change: build a review step into how often the pack's contact sheet is updated
pearls: Involve the Admiral Nurse or dementia support worker (where available) in designing and distributing the information pack
Use nationally available dementia information resources (e.g. from a recognised dementia charity) rather than creating leaflets from scratch
Present the audit to the memory service's multidisciplinary team so the change is owned by whoever gives the diagnosis, not just doctors
Track whether patients/carers can name their named contact at a follow-up appointment, as a simple outcome check
Repeat the audit after any change of memory service staff or information pack version
effort: ~15 min per 10 records from the memory service record
pass: Both oral discussion and a written information resource covering subtype, expected changes and contact details are documented as given at the diagnosis appointment

question: Do people living with dementia have a single named health or social care professional recorded who is responsible for coordinating their care?
why: No audit in the library measures whether a single named care coordinator is documented for people with dementia, despite this being an explicit NICE requirement and a recognised driver of fragmented care in old age psychiatry.

standard.source: NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers, rec 1.3.1 (2018)
standard.wording: Provide people living with dementia with a single named health or social care professional who is responsible for coordinating their care.

population: Inclusion: adults with a confirmed dementia diagnosis open to old age psychiatry or memory service follow-up. Exclusion: patients discharged back to primary care with no ongoing specialist follow-up.
sample: 30 consecutive patients with dementia currently open to the old age psychiatry/memory service caseload
data_source: Old age psychiatry/memory service electronic care record
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'named care coordinator' field to the dementia care plan template, updated automatically whenever the case is transferred between workers
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the old age psychiatry/memory service governance meeting; if effective, embed the mandatory field permanently
evidence: Related library entries concern old age psychiatry new patient assessment quality, but no audit yet checks the specific named-coordinator requirement in NG97
pitfalls: A team name (e.g. 'memory service') rather than an individual should not count as a pass: define 'named' strictly as a specific person
Coordinators may change with staff turnover without a corresponding record update: check the last reviewed date, not just presence of a name
Patients under both a GP and a specialist service may have two different coordinators without either being aware: flag and record this as a fail
Caseload lists may include patients who have moved out of area or died: verify the current caseload with the team manager before sampling
A coordinator listed only on paper records, not the electronic system, may be missed: check both if the service uses hybrid records
pearls: Work with the memory service's care coordinator role holders (often community psychiatric nurses) to design the mandatory field
Use a case transfer checklist that requires updating the named coordinator field whenever a case moves between workers
Present the audit alongside the annual health check and key worker audits for learning disability, since the underlying principle (a single accountable named person) is shared
Track patient/carer awareness of who their named coordinator is at a follow-up visit, as a simple outcome check
Repeat the audit after any staffing changes in the service, since this is when coordination is most likely to be lost
effort: ~10 min per 10 records from the memory service record
pass: A single named individual (not a team name) with a role and contact method is documented as the care coordinator in the current care record

question: Do adults referred to a memory assessment service have anticholinergic burden from their current medicines documented as part of the reversible-causes work-up before a diagnosis of dementia is confirmed?
why: The anticholinergic burden review topic card in the library (5 audits) shows scores are calculated but action rarely follows; no audit in the library checks anticholinergic burden specifically as part of the pre-diagnosis reversible-causes assessment that NICE requires before confirming dementia.

standard.source: NICE NG97 Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers, rec 1.2.6 (2018)
standard.wording: ...refer them to a specialist dementia diagnostic service (such as a memory clinic or community old age psychiatry service) if: reversible causes of cognitive decline (including delirium, depression, sensory impairment [such as sight or hearing loss] or cognitive impairment from medicines associated with increased anticholinergic burden) have been investigated and dementia is still suspected.

population: Inclusion: adults assessed by the memory assessment service in the audit period, ending in a confirmed dementia diagnosis. Exclusion: assessments where dementia was excluded (reversible cause found and treated).
sample: 30 consecutive new dementia diagnoses over the last 6 months, from the memory assessment service
data_source: Memory assessment service electronic record and medication review documentation
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic anticholinergic burden score calculation to the memory assessment service's pre-diagnosis work-up template, pulling from the current medication list, with a mandatory action field when the score is high
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the memory assessment service and pharmacy governance meeting; if effective, embed the automatic calculation permanently
evidence: Topic card 'Anticholinergic burden review': 75.4% of patients with an ACB score of 3 or more had no documented intervention [3536]; 24% with ACB over 3 had no assessment at all [3428]; consultant advice recommends building the score into the workflow and auditing whether a medication change follows a high score, rather than measuring the score alone again
pitfalls: A high ACB score with no action documented should count as a fail, even if the score itself was calculated: audit the action, not just the calculation, per consultant advice

Some anticholinergic medicines may be prescribed by another specialty (e.g. urology, gastroenterology) and not visible to the memory service: request a full GP medication list, not just psychiatric medicines
Stopping a medicine started for a good clinical reason may not be appropriate: a documented reason for continuing should count as a pass, not just a stop or switch
The library shows the only closed loop for this topic got worse at re-audit [3388]: monitor closely after any change rather than assuming a single intervention will hold
Retrospective identification of anticholinergic burden calculations may be difficult if not consistently coded: consider prospective data collection via the new automatic field instead
pearls: Build the ACB calculator directly into the memory assessment pre-diagnosis template so it is not a separate, easily skipped step
Involve a memory service pharmacist to review any high-score cases and recommend action, closing the loop the corpus shows is currently missing
Use the topic card's finding that a previous closed loop got worse at re-audit [3388] to argue for embedding the fix in the system rather than relying on a single education cycle
Present both the ACB score and the resulting action rate together, since scoring alone (without action) is already common practice
Repeat the audit at 6 months specifically to check whether action rates (not just scoring rates) have genuinely improved
effort: ~15 min per 10 records from the memory assessment record
pass: An anticholinergic burden score (or explicit medication review for anticholinergic drugs) is documented before a dementia diagnosis is confirmed

question: Are adults in acute alcohol withdrawal assessed immediately on admission to hospital by a healthcare professional skilled in the management of alcohol withdrawal?
why: The alcohol withdrawal management topic card in the library (8 audits) shows scoring tool use is the well-studied weak point; no audit in the library isolates the separate, more basic requirement that a skilled professional assesses the patient immediately on admission, which is a precondition for using any scoring tool correctly.

standard.source: NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications, rec 1.1.2.3 (2010)
standard.wording: People in acute alcohol withdrawal should be assessed immediately on admission to hospital by a healthcare professional skilled in the management of alcohol withdrawal.

population: Inclusion: adults admitted to a medical or surgical ward with acute alcohol withdrawal or a high risk of it, identified by alcohol history or admission coding. Exclusion: patients admitted primarily for another condition with no withdrawal risk identified.
sample: 30 consecutive adults admitted with acute alcohol withdrawal risk over the last 3 months
data_source: Admission clerking record and addiction/alcohol liaison team referral log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic referral to the alcohol/addiction liaison team triggered by any admission coded with an alcohol withdrawal risk flag, with a target response time built into the referral system
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the addiction liaison and acute medicine governance meeting; if effective, embed the automatic referral trigger permanently
evidence: Topic card 'Alcohol withdrawal management': addiction specialist oversight on acute wards was as low as 4% [3275], showing that specialist/skilled assessment itself (not just scoring) is a recognised gap; a ward SOP with nurse-administered CIWA-Ar after team training achieved full risk stratification and symptom-triggered dosing at re-audit [3299]
pitfalls: A generic admitting doctor with no specific alcohol withdrawal training may be wrongly counted as 'skilled': define this role explicitly with the addiction liaison team before data collection
Out-of-hours admissions may have no immediate access to a specialist assessor: record and report out-of-hours performance separately
Alcohol withdrawal risk may not be identified at all on admission if the history is incomplete: this audit should separately note where risk was missed entirely, as a more serious finding
A busy acute medical unit may triage alcohol withdrawal as lower priority than other presentations: highlight the safety rationale (risk of seizures, delirium tremens) in any change
Small numbers in a quieter unit: extend the collection window if fewer than 20 cases are found in 3 months
pearls: Use the existing alcohol liaison team's own referral log as a secondary data source to cross-check ward documentation
Present the corpus finding that a ward SOP with training (not just a scoring tool) achieved full compliance [3299], to support investment in a similar local SOP
Recruit an acute medicine consultant alongside the addiction liaison lead, since assessment timing depends on acute take processes
Track out-of-hours versus in-hours compliance separately, since this is likely to reveal the biggest gap
Fix the re-audit date at 3 months to check whether an automatic referral trigger, once built, is being used consistently
effort: ~15 min per 10 admissions from the clerking and liaison referral record
pass: An assessment by a professional documented as skilled in alcohol withdrawal management (e.g. addiction liaison nurse, specialist doctor) is recorded within 4 hours of admission

question: What proportion of adults treated for acute alcohol withdrawal have their withdrawal severity monitored using a structured, validated tool (such as CIWA-Ar or GMAWS), completed and scored at the frequency specified in the local protocol?
why: The alcohol withdrawal management topic card in the library shows CIWA-Ar completion rates as low as 1% within 24 hours [3603] and correctly scored in only 24% [3286]; this audit targets whether the tool is actually completed and scored at the required frequency, distinct from the existing corpus focus on whether a symptom-triggered benzodiazepine regimen is prescribed.

standard.source: NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications, rec 1.1.2.2 (2010)
standard.wording: Follow locally specified protocols to assess and monitor patients in acute alcohol withdrawal. Consider using a tool (such as the Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment - Alcohol, revised [CIWA-Ar] scale) as an adjunct to clinical judgement.

population: Inclusion: adults admitted with acute alcohol withdrawal and started on a symptom-triggered or fixed-dose benzodiazepine regimen. Exclusion: patients managed entirely in a specialist inpatient detoxification unit with a different established protocol already closely audited.
sample: 30 consecutive adults treated for acute alcohol withdrawal on a general medical/surgical ward over the last 3 months
data_source: Ward observation chart and drug chart
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Replace the free-text withdrawal observation chart with an integrated electronic CIWA-Ar/GMAWS chart that calculates the score automatically from entered items and flags missed or overdue scores
reaudit: At 3 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the addiction liaison and ward nursing governance meeting; if effective, adopt the electronic chart trust-wide
evidence: Topic card 'Alcohol withdrawal management': CIWA within 24 hours was 1% in one trust [3603], CIWA-Ar completed in 23.97% [3551], and applied with correct scoring in only 24% [3286]; repeated re-audits at one trust barely moved (1%, then 4%, then 17%) [3603], showing teaching alone is insufficient and a structural (electronic) fix is needed
pitfalls: A withdrawal scoring tool used inconsistently (e.g. only at night) may look complete on a single spot-check: audit the full expected schedule over 48 hours, not a single time point
Incorrect scoring (miscounted items) is common per the library findings: sample a subset for scoring accuracy by an independent reviewer, not just presence of a score
Ward staff turnover and unfamiliarity with the tool contribute to poor completion: pair any electronic chart rollout with brief mandatory training
The library shows repeated re-audits with teaching alone made only small gains: do not repeat a teaching-only cycle without a structural change
Patients transferred to a specialist detox unit partway through admission should have their general ward period audited separately from the specialist unit period
pearls: Use the corpus finding that a ward SOP with nurse-administered CIWA-Ar and team training achieved full risk stratification at re-audit [3299] as the template for the local change
Build automatic scoring calculation into the electronic system so nurses do not need to add up items manually, reducing the correct-scoring gap found in the corpus
Recruit ward nursing leads as co-audit leads, since they complete the chart in practice
Present the corpus's repeated-failure finding [3603] to justify prioritising an electronic fix over another teaching cycle
Track whether correct, frequent scoring changes the benzodiazepine dose given (symptom-triggered dosing), linking this audit to safer prescribing
effort: ~15 min per 10 admissions from the ward observation and drug chart
pass: A CIWA-Ar (or locally approved equivalent) score is recorded at the frequency specified in the local protocol for at least the first 48 hours of admission or until withdrawal resolves

question: What proportion of adults with decompensated liver disease being treated for acute alcohol withdrawal have a documented plan agreed with, or advice sought from, a healthcare professional experienced in liver disease?
why: No audit in the library checks this specific NICE safety requirement for the highest-risk subgroup of alcohol withdrawal patients (those with decompensated liver disease), despite general alcohol withdrawal management being audited extensively.

standard.source: NICE CG100 Alcohol-use disorders: diagnosis and management of physical complications, rec 1.1.3.2 (2010, amended 2021)
standard.wording: People with decompensated liver disease who are being treated for acute alcohol withdrawal should be offered advice from a healthcare professional experienced in the management of liver disease...

population: Inclusion: adults with a diagnosis of decompensated liver disease (ascites, jaundice, encephalopathy or variceal bleeding) treated for acute alcohol withdrawal. Exclusion: patients with alcohol-related liver disease but no current decompensation.
sample: All identified cases in the last 12 months (numbers are likely to be small, 10-20 cases, in a district general hospital; extend the window if fewer are found)
data_source: Medical admission and hepatology/gastroenterology referral records
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic hepatology/gastroenterology referral trigger to the electronic alcohol withdrawal order set whenever decompensated liver disease is coded alongside alcohol withdrawal treatment
reaudit: At 12 months, same template, widened window if numbers remain small
close_loop: Present at the joint hepatology/addiction liaison governance meeting; if effective, embed the automatic referral trigger permanently
evidence: No audit specific to liver specialist involvement in alcohol withdrawal with decompensated liver disease is recorded in the library; the nearest related entries concern general alcohol withdrawal scoring and symptom-triggered regimens, which do not address this specific high-risk subgroup
pitfalls: Decompensated liver disease may not be clearly coded, especially if the presentation is dominated by withdrawal symptoms: cross-check liver function tests and clinical notes, not just the coding system
Advice may be given informally by phone without a written record: require the advice or plan to be documented in the notes regardless of how it was obtained
Choice of sedative may need adjustment in liver failure (e.g. shorter-acting benzodiazepines): record whether the medication choice reflects this, as a secondary marker of specialist input
Numbers will be small: consider a 12-month or longer collection window and report raw numbers alongside any percentage
Weekend and out-of-hours presentations may have delayed access to liver specialist advice: record and report time-of-week separately
pearls: Recruit a hepatology or gastroenterology liaison consultant as a joint audit lead with addiction liaison psychiatry
Use liver function tests and coding together to build a more complete case-finding search than either alone
Present the audit as protecting a small, very high-risk group, to secure engagement despite the modest case numbers
Build the electronic referral trigger to also suggest a liver-safe benzodiazepine choice, closing two safety gaps at once
Keep this as an ongoing, rolling audit given the low case volume, rather than a single fixed 3-month cycle
effort: ~20 min per identified case from the medical and hepatology record
pass: Advice from, or a joint plan with, a healthcare professional experienced in liver disease (hepatology, gastroenterology or a liver-specialist nurse) is documented within 24 hours of decompensated liver disease being identified during alcohol withdrawal treatment

question: What proportion of patients discharged from inpatient drug treatment services (including specialist community and inpatient detoxification services) after treatment for opioid use are supplied with take-home naloxone, or have a documented reason why not?
why: No audit in the library measures naloxone supply on discharge from inpatient drug treatment settings, despite national guidance permitting a wide range of drug treatment services, including inpatient services, to supply naloxone without a prescription to reduce overdose deaths.

standard.source: GOV.UK Supplying take home naloxone without a prescription (Human Medicines Regulations 2012, regulation 238; guidance updated 12 September 2025)
standard.wording: The types of drug treatment services that can supply naloxone include, but may not be limited to: drug services provided by primary care services; drug services provided by secondary care services (including a range of specialised community and inpatient drug services)...

population: Inclusion: adults discharged from an inpatient drug/alcohol treatment unit or psychiatric ward following treatment where opioid use was part of the presentation. Exclusion: patients with no history of opioid use in the current or past 12 months.
sample: 30 consecutive discharges with a history of opioid use from the inpatient drug treatment or dual diagnosis service over the last 6 months
data_source: Inpatient drug treatment service discharge record and pharmacy dispensing log
timeline: Wk 1-2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5-12 embed; Wk 13-14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory 'naloxone supplied or reason not supplied' field to the inpatient drug treatment discharge checklist, which cannot be completed without an entry, and stock take-home naloxone kits on the ward
reaudit: At 6 months, same template and sample
close_loop: Present at the drug treatment service and pharmacy governance meeting; if effective, embed the mandatory field and ward stock as standard practice
evidence: [1341] Audit of safe opioid prescribing across surgical departments found naloxone co-prescribing improved from below 50% to over 70% in several departments after education and reminders, showing naloxone supply is a modifiable, auditable practice even though this specific audit is in a surgical rather than drug treatment context
pitfalls: Patients may already hold a naloxone kit from a community drug service: record this as a valid reason for non-supply rather than a fail
Ward staff may be unfamiliar with the legal basis for supplying naloxone without an individual prescription: provide brief training alongside the mandatory field
Family members or carers present at discharge may also need training in use, which is easy to miss if only the patient is addressed
Stock and expiry management of naloxone kits on the ward needs a named responsible person, or supply will lapse
A patient who leaves against medical advice before formal discharge may miss the opportunity for supply: consider a rapid-access naloxone offer earlier in the admission for high-risk patients
pearls: Partner with the local community drug and alcohol service, which will already have a naloxone supply protocol that can be adapted for inpatient use
Use the gov.uk guidance's explicit inclusion of inpatient drug services to reassure ward staff of the legal basis for supply without an individual prescription
Build training on naloxone use into existing discharge planning conversations rather than as a separate appointment
Track whether kits supplied are ever used (via ambulance service or community data, where locally available) as a longer-term outcome measure
Keep a standing stock of naloxone kits on the ward with a named pharmacy lead responsible for restocking and expiry checks
effort: ~10 min per 10 discharges from the discharge checklist and pharmacy log
pass: A take-home naloxone kit is documented as supplied at discharge, or a specific reason for not supplying it (e.g. already holds a kit, clinically inappropriate, declined) is recorded
